territories.name: Straits Settlements
territories.formalName: The Colony of the Straits Settlements

geoCoverage.label: Penang, Malacca and Singapore
With Labuan
geoCoverage.change: Labuan, off the Borneo coast and 1,300 km away, was transferred from the British North Borneo Company and attached to the colony as a fourth settlement.

acquisitions.how: The East India Company merged three stations it already held — Penang, taken from Kedah in 1786; Malacca, traded from the Dutch in 1824; and Singapore, bought from the Sultan of Johor in 1824 — into one government answering to Calcutta.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of the Netherlands
counterparties.lost: Every Dutch claim north of the Singapore Strait, given up in the 1824 Treaty of London in exchange for Bencoolen and a free hand in Sumatra.

counterparties.name: The Johor-Riau Sultanate
counterparties.lost: Its unity. The 1824 line put the peninsula and Singapore under Britain and the Riau-Lingga islands under the Dutch, dividing one maritime kingdom between two European empires and, eventually, two modern countries.

instrument.name: Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 (Treaty of London)
instrument.note: The treaty made the union possible by settling which European power claimed which side of the Straits.

acquisitions.how: Labuan, which the British North Borneo Company had run badly since 1890, was taken off the company and attached to the Straits Settlements as a fourth, distant settlement.

counterparties.name: The British North Borneo Company
counterparties.lost: Administration of an island it had never made pay; the Colonial Office judged the company had let Labuan's coal trade and its courts fall apart.

statusPeriods.label: East India Company presidency, then residency
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A shareholder company in London governed three ports through a Governor at Penang and, from 1832, at Singapore; the settlements were a Presidency until 1830 and then a residency subordinate to Bengal.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Penang to 1832, then Singapore, under Calcutta

statusPeriods.label: Ruled from India by the Crown
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: When the Crown abolished Company rule in India the Straits went with it, governed from Calcutta by an Indian administration that knew nothing about the Malay world and taxed the settlements to pay for it.
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. Singapore's merchants petitioned Parliament from 1857 to be moved to the Colonial Office, and won.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony under the Colonial Office
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Governor at Singapore ruled with an Executive and a nominated Legislative Council, and from 1896 the same man was also High Commissioner for the Malay States — one official holding the colony and the protectorates together.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Singapore, under the Colonial Office in London
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. Chinese, Indian and European unofficial members were appointed by the Governor.
statusPeriods.note: The colony also administered outposts far outside the Straits: the Dindings on the Perak coast from 1874 to 1935, Christmas Island from 1900 and the Cocos-Keeling Islands from 1903, both of which were transferred to Australia in the 1950s.

statusPeriods.label: Japanese occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Japan held all four settlements, ran Singapore as Syonan-to, and in 1943 handed Malaya's four northern states to Thailand as a reward for alliance.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Enemy occupation; British authority was zero. Modelled per the data model's rule for occupation by another power.

statusPeriods.label: British Military Administration
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Army officers ran the settlements for seven months amid food shortages, inflation and strikes, while London prepared to abolish the colony altogether.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Singapore, under South East Asia Command

departures.how: Britain abolished the colony and dealt out its parts: Penang and Malacca into the new Malayan Union, Labuan into North Borneo, and Singapore kept back as a separate colony because its Chinese majority would have outnumbered the Malays in any federation.

becomes.name: Malayan Union, later the Federation of Malaya

led.name: Harold MacMichael
led.role: special envoy who collected the Malay rulers' signatures for the new arrangement in six weeks, some under threat of deposition

led.name: Onn Jaafar
led.role: Johor civil servant who organised the Malay protest against the Malayan Union and founded UMNO on 11 May 1946

led.name: Edward Gent
led.role: first and last Governor of the Malayan Union

cost.note: Nobody died. This was a reorganisation, not a decolonisation: every part of the old colony stayed under British rule, and the separation of Singapore from Malaya set up the quarrel that ended in 1965.

departures.borders: The 1946 carve-up drew the border that still matters most in the region: Singapore on one side, the peninsula on the other, a line made for demographic arithmetic and never undone.

populationTransfer.note: The settlements were the gateway for Chinese and Indian migration into the Malay world: by 1931 the Straits Settlements were about 60 per cent Chinese, and Malaya as a whole was close to being a country where Malays were not the majority.

consequences.borderLegacy: Two of the region's borders came out of this colony: the Malaysia-Indonesia line drawn by the 1824 treaty, and the Malaysia-Singapore line drawn by the 1946 dissolution.
consequences.economicLegacy: Free ports with no tariffs and no customs made the Straits the collecting point for the tin and rubber of the peninsula and the produce of the archipelago; the colony's revenue came instead from government monopolies on opium, which supplied up to half of it in some years.

commonwealth.note: Through its successors, Malaysia and Singapore.

peak.populationNote: 1931 census of the Straits Settlements, rounded. Singapore held more than half of it.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Straits Settlements’s largest recorded population: 1,114,000 people, counted in 1931.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: C. M. Turnbull
evidence.work: The Straits Settlements 1826-67: Indian Presidency to Crown Colony
evidence.supports: The formation of the colony, Indian rule and the 1867 transfer.

evidence.author: Carl A. Trocki
evidence.work: Opium, Empire and the Global Political Economy: A Study of the Asian Opium Trade 1750-1950
evidence.supports: The opium revenue farms that financed the Straits Settlements.

evidence.author: Barbara Watson Andaya and Leonard Y. Andaya
evidence.work: A History of Malaysia
evidence.supports: The colony's relations with the Malay states and its 1946 dissolution.

pedagogy.hook: Up to half of this colony's government revenue came from selling opium to Chinese labourers — the same drug Britain had fought two wars to force into China.

misconception.belief: British colonies paid for themselves through trade.
misconception.correction: The Straits Settlements were free ports and collected almost no customs duty. What paid for the police, the courts and the harbour was the government opium monopoly, farmed out to Chinese syndicates, which in some years supplied between 40 and 60 per cent of revenue. The colony was funded by addiction among the workers it imported.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: This is where British power in South-East Asia was based for 120 years, and it is the clearest example anywhere in the empire of a colony whose finances rested on a drug monopoly. It also shows how administrative decisions draw borders: two of the region's frontiers were made in this colony's paperwork.

territories.name: Penang
territories.formalName: Settlement of Penang (Prince of Wales Island and Province Wellesley)

from.note: The Malay name — 'betel-nut island' — is older than any surviving record of it.

namesOverTime.name: Prince of Wales Island
namesOverTime.note: Francis Light took possession on the Prince of Wales's birthday and named the island after him. Malays went on calling it Pulau Pinang throughout.

modernSuccessors.name: Malaysia (state of Pulau Pinang)
modernSuccessors.note: A state of the Federation of Malaya from 1957 and of Malaysia from 1963. The federal government still pays Kedah RM10,000 a year for it.

geoCoverage.label: The island, and from 1800 the mainland strip opposite
geoCoverage.change: The drawn shape is the modern state of Pulau Pinang. It cannot be split into the island taken in 1786 and Province Wellesley, the mainland strip taken from Kedah in 1800.

acquisitions.how: Francis Light of the East India Company took an almost empty island from Sultan Abdullah Mukarram Shah of Kedah by promising him British protection against Siam and Burma — a promise Light had no authority to give and the Company never kept.

counterparties.name: Sultanate of Kedah
counterparties.lost: Kedah lost the island in 1786 and the mainland strip of Province Wellesley in 1800, and got neither the army nor the alliance it had bargained for; in 1821 a Siamese invasion drove its Sultan into exile in Penang while the British watched.
counterparties.note: Kedah accepted a rent instead: 6,000 Spanish dollars a year from 1791, raised to 10,000 in 1800. Malaysia's federal government still pays that sum, now RM10,000, to Kedah every year.

instrument.name: Treaty of Friendship and Alliance between the East India Company and the Sultan of Kedah
instrument.note: The 1786 occupation rested on an unratified agreement. Kedah tried to take the island back by force in 1791, was beaten, and signed this treaty accepting an annual payment instead.

people.name: Francis Light
people.role: country trader turned Company superintendent; occupied the island and founded George Town

people.name: Sultan Abdullah Mukarram Shah
people.role: ruler of Kedah who granted the island in exchange for military protection he never received

acquisitions.resistance: Kedah massed boats and men at Prai in 1791 to retake the island; Light attacked first, scattered them, and imposed the treaty that turned a broken bargain into a rent.

evidence.author: Nordin Hussin
evidence.work: Trade and Society in the Straits of Melaka: Dutch Melaka and English Penang, 1780-1830
evidence.supports: The terms Light offered Kedah, the 1791 fighting and the rent settlement.

statusPeriods.label: East India Company settlement
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A London shareholder company owned the island, appointed its superintendent and later its Governor, and ran it first from Calcutta, then briefly as a Presidency in its own right from 1805, then from Calcutta again.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: George Town, under Fort William in Calcutta
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. The Company's Recorder's Court, set up in 1807, was the only check on the Governor.
statusPeriods.note: In 1805 Penang was made the Company's Fourth Presidency, on a par with Bengal, Madras and Bombay, in the expectation it would become a great naval base. It never did, and the rank was stripped away in 1830.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony, Straits Settlements
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Crown took the Company's possessions in 1858 and ruled Penang through the Government of India until 1 April 1867, when the Colonial Office took it over as part of the crown colony of the Straits Settlements.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Singapore, under the Colonial Office in London
statusPeriods.franchise: No elections until 1948. The Straits Settlements Legislative Council was appointed, with a handful of unofficial members chosen from Chinese, Indian and European merchants.
statusPeriods.note: Penang's Chinese and Indian merchant families made it the busiest port in the northern Straits; George Town's shophouse grid is the physical record of that trade.

statusPeriods.label: Japanese occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Japan took Penang on 19 December 1941 after the British evacuated the European population by sea and left everyone else behind — a decision Asians in Malaya never forgot.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Occupied by Japan: British authority was zero for three years and nine months. The status is 'occupied' with degree 0, following the model's rule for enemy occupation.

statusPeriods.label: Settlement of the Federation of Malaya
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British military government ran Penang until April 1946; it was then a settlement of the Malayan Union and, from 1 February 1948, of the Federation of Malaya, with a British High Commissioner in Kuala Lumpur above its Resident Commissioner.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kuala Lumpur and George Town, under the Colonial Office
statusPeriods.franchise: George Town elected Malaya's first municipal council in December 1951; the first federal elections followed in 1955, on a register that excluded most non-citizens.
statusPeriods.note: Between 1948 and 1951 a Penang Secession Committee of Chinese, Indian and Eurasian businessmen petitioned London to keep the island out of the Federation. The Colonial Office refused even to reply formally.

departures.how: Penang became independent not on its own but as one of eleven states of the Federation of Malaya, after London conceded elections in 1955 and a constitutional conference in January 1956.

led.name: Tunku Abdul Rahman
led.role: Chief Minister of Malaya; led the London talks that fixed the date

led.name: Wong Pow Nee
led.role: first Chief Minister of Penang, 1957; argued the island's future lay inside Malaya, not outside it

led.name: Heah Joo Seang
led.role: Penang businessman who led the 1948-51 secession campaign against joining the Federation

cost.note: Nobody died at independence in Penang. The killing in Malaya had happened during the Emergency of 1948-60, which was still running on the day the flag changed.

departures.borders: Penang's borders did not move, but its status did: a free port under London became a state under Kuala Lumpur, and its free-port privileges were finally abolished in 1969.

populationTransfer.note: Light declared Penang a free port with no customs and no religious restrictions, and within twenty years Malay, Chinese, Tamil, Acehnese, Arab and Armenian traders had built a town of about 12,000 people on an island that had held a few hundred.

commonwealth.note: As part of Malaya and then Malaysia. Malaysia's head of state is its own elected king, the Yang di-Pertuan Agong.

consequences.economicLegacy: A free port for 180 years, Penang lost that status in 1969 and rebuilt itself around electronics assembly; George Town's colonial-era shophouse core became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2008.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English common law, an English-medium school system that produced much of Malaya's first political generation, and street names still bearing the surnames of Chinese and British merchants side by side.

peak.populationNote: 1947 Malayan census for the Settlement of Penang, rounded. Chinese residents were the largest group, then Malays and Indians.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Penang’s largest recorded population: 446,000 people, counted in 1947.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

areaWarrant.author: This atlas, measuring the ground it draws
areaWarrant.work: app/data/geo/units.index.json — Natural Earth 1:10m admin boundaries, measured on a sphere of radius 6,371 km by tools/build-geo.js
areaWarrant.supports: Penang’s greatest extent, 1,048 km² in 1957: the 1 map unit this atlas draws it holding that year measure 1,023 km², within 2.4% of it.
areaWarrant.check: Open the atlas at that year and select this territory: the outline you see IS the figure. Its units are listed under `geoCoverage` in the shard and measured in app/data/geo/units.index.json, from Natural Earth 1:10m boundaries — public domain, naturalearthdata.com.
areaWarrant.note: A modern outline measured to check an older figure. It confirms the size and the shape to within a twentieth; it is not the surveyed border of that year, and no colonial border was ever surveyed to that precision anyway.

evidence.author: Barbara Watson Andaya and Leonard Y. Andaya
evidence.work: A History of Malaysia
evidence.supports: Penang's founding, the Kedah bargain and its place in the Straits Settlements.

evidence.author: Nordin Hussin
evidence.work: Trade and Society in the Straits of Melaka: Dutch Melaka and English Penang, 1780-1830
evidence.supports: Penang's population, trade and free-port policy in its first fifty years.

evidence.author: C. M. Turnbull
evidence.work: The Straits Settlements 1826-67: Indian Presidency to Crown Colony
evidence.supports: Penang's demotion from Presidency and the 1867 transfer to the Colonial Office.

pedagogy.hook: Malaysia still posts Kedah a cheque for RM10,000 every year. It is rent for Penang, agreed in 1800, and no government has ever dared stop paying it.

misconception.belief: Penang was an empty island that the British found and developed, so nobody lost anything.
misconception.correction: The island was thinly peopled, but it belonged to Kedah, and Kedah gave it up for a defence promise Francis Light knew the Company would not honour. When Siam invaded Kedah in 1821 the British in Penang did nothing, and the Sultan spent years as a refugee in the town built on his island.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Penang is where the British empire in South-East Asia starts, and it starts with a private trader making a promise on behalf of a company that had not agreed to it. Almost every later Malayan treaty follows the same shape: protection offered, sovereignty taken.

Kedah cedes Province Wellesley; the rent rises to 10,000 Spanish dollars
Joined with Malacca and Singapore as the Straits Settlements
Japan takes Penang after the British evacuate Europeans only

territories.name: Singapore
territories.formalName: Colony of Singapore

from.note: Fourteenth-century Chinese and Javanese sources name a trading settlement here; excavation at Fort Canning has confirmed it.

to.note: The settlement was sacked and abandoned around 1400; the date is archaeological, not documentary.

namesOverTime.name: Singapura

from.note: The name appears in the Sejarah Melayu and in Portuguese accounts; its adoption cannot be dated precisely.

namesOverTime.note: 'Lion city', from Sanskrit. The island was a minor settlement of the Johor sultanate under a Temenggong when Raffles arrived.

modernSuccessors.name: Republic of Singapore
modernSuccessors.note: British to 1963, a state of Malaysia for 23 months, and a sovereign republic since it was expelled on 9 August 1965.

geoCoverage.label: The island and its islets
geoCoverage.change: The 1824 treaty extended the settlement from a strip of coast to the whole island and everything within ten miles of it.

acquisitions.how: Stamford Raffles and William Farquhar landed on an island of perhaps a thousand people, recognised Tengku Hussein as Sultan of Johor against his reigning brother, and were granted the right to build a trading post in return.

counterparties.name: The Johor-Riau Sultanate
counterparties.lost: Its succession was decided by a foreign company: Raffles installed a claimant who would sign, and in doing so split the sultanate into a British half and a Dutch half.
counterparties.note: The reigning Sultan, Abdul Rahman, was in Dutch-controlled Riau. Raffles simply recognised his elder brother instead.

counterparties.name: The Orang Laut and Malay inhabitants of Singapore
counterparties.lost: The island's sea-people communities lost their fishing grounds and their villages to the new town within a generation, and their descendants were resettled ashore.
counterparties.note: Raffles's own account gives about 1,000 people on the island in 1819, most of them Orang Laut and Malays under the Temenggong.

instrument.name: Preliminary Agreement between Raffles, Sultan Hussein Shah and Temenggong Abdul Rahman
instrument.note: The agreement granted only a trading post and annual payments, not sovereignty. Sovereignty came five years later.

people.name: Stamford Raffles
people.role: Lieutenant-Governor of Bencoolen; chose the site and dictated the terms

people.name: William Farquhar
people.role: first Resident, who actually built the settlement and was later written out of its story by Raffles

people.name: Tengku Hussein (Sultan Hussein Shah)
people.role: recognised as Sultan of Johor by the British in exchange for the treaty

people.name: Temenggong Abdul Rahman
people.role: the island's actual ruler, who signed and took an allowance

contested.note: Whether Raffles 'founded' Singapore is disputed. Archaeology at Fort Canning shows a substantial fourteenth-century port; the National Museum now dates the city's history from 1299, not 1819. What Raffles founded was a British free port on a site that had been a trading settlement before.

evidence.author: C. M. Turnbull
evidence.work: A History of Modern Singapore, 1819-2005
evidence.supports: The 1819 landing, the succession manoeuvre and the terms of the agreement.

acquisitions.how: John Crawfurd bought the whole island outright for 33,200 Spanish dollars in cash plus monthly pensions, converting a rented factory into British sovereign territory.

counterparties.name: Sultan Hussein Shah and Temenggong Abdul Rahman
counterparties.lost: Full sovereignty over Singapore and every island within ten miles of it, in exchange for a lump sum and pensions of 1,300 and 700 Spanish dollars a month; both men and their heirs became salaried residents of a town they had once ruled.

instrument.name: Treaty of Friendship and Alliance (the Crawfurd Treaty)

people.name: John Crawfurd
people.role: Resident who negotiated the outright cession

statusPeriods.label: East India Company factory
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Company held a trading post by permission of a Sultan it had itself installed, on a lease it paid for annually, while London argued about whether Raffles had exceeded his authority.

statusPeriods.label: Company settlement and Straits capital
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The East India Company owned and governed the island, made it the capital of the Straits Settlements in 1832, and left it almost entirely to run itself as a free port with no customs and no direct taxes.
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. Merchants petitioned instead, and in the 1850s campaigned openly to be taken away from Indian rule.
statusPeriods.note: Singapore's population went from about 1,000 in 1819 to over 80,000 by 1860, most of them Chinese migrants arriving through a credit-ticket system that left them in debt to the brokers who shipped them.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony and imperial naval base
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Crown took over from the Company in 1858 and the Colonial Office from the Government of India on 1 April 1867; a Governor ruled with a nominated Legislative Council, and after 1923 the island carried Britain's main naval base east of Suez.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Singapore, under the Colonial Office in London
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. Unofficial members of the Legislative Council were appointed from the merchant communities.
statusPeriods.note: The Singapore Naval Base, opened in 1938 at a cost of about sixty million pounds, was built on the assumption that any attack would come from the sea.

statusPeriods.label: Japanese occupation as Syonan-to
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Japan renamed the island Syonan-to, 'light of the south', ran it under military government, and within a fortnight of the surrender began the Sook Ching screening that killed thousands of Chinese men.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Enemy occupation: British authority was zero for three and a half years. Modelled as 'occupied' with degree 0 under the data model's rule.

statusPeriods.label: Separate crown colony
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain detached Singapore from the rest of Malaya on 1 April 1946 and kept it as a separate colony, largely because its Chinese majority would have unbalanced any Malayan federation; elections were conceded in stages from 1948.
statusPeriods.franchise: Six elected seats in 1948 on a British-subject register of about 23,000; automatic registration and a mass electorate came only with the 1955 Rendel constitution.
statusPeriods.note: David Marshall became the first Chief Minister in 1955 and resigned in 1956 when London refused full internal self-government; Lim Yew Hock's crackdown on the Chinese middle-school and union left followed.

statusPeriods.label: Internal self-government under Lee Kuan Yew
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Singaporeans elected their own government and Lee Kuan Yew became Prime Minister; Britain kept defence, foreign affairs and a veto on internal security exercised through a joint council with Malaya.
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage with compulsory voting from 1959.
statusPeriods.note: The 1 September 1962 merger referendum offered three kinds of merger and no option to reject it; 71 per cent chose the government's terms and about a quarter of ballots were left blank in protest.

departures.how: Singapore left the British empire not on its own but by joining Malaysia, because both Lee Kuan Yew and London believed an independent Chinese-majority island could not survive economically or resist a communist takeover.

led.name: Lee Kuan Yew
led.role: Prime Minister; campaigned for merger as the only route out of colonial rule

led.name: Lim Chin Siong
led.role: trade union leader of the Barisan Sosialis, who opposed merger on the terms offered and was detained without trial in Operation Coldstore in February 1963

led.name: Tunku Abdul Rahman
led.role: Prime Minister of Malaya, who accepted Singapore only alongside Sabah and Sarawak to keep the racial arithmetic

cost.note: On 2 February 1963 Operation Coldstore detained about 110 opposition politicians, unionists and journalists without trial in the run-up to merger. Britain, Malaya and Singapore's own government jointly authorised it; the last of those detained was released in 1982.

departures.borders: Singapore's own boundaries were unchanged, but its constitutional position was not: it entered Malaysia with control of education and labour and only 15 seats in the federal parliament, an arrangement that broke down within two years.

instrument.name: Malaysia Agreement 1963
instrument.note: Signed in London by Britain, Malaya, Singapore, North Borneo and Sarawak. Malaysia Day was postponed from 31 August to 16 September to allow a United Nations mission to test opinion in Borneo.

evidence.author: C. M. Turnbull
evidence.work: A History of Modern Singapore, 1819-2005
evidence.supports: The merger campaign, the referendum and the terms of entry into Malaysia.

populationTransfer.note: Free entry and the credit-ticket system brought hundreds of thousands of Chinese and Indian migrants through Singapore in the nineteenth century; by 1860 the Chinese were a majority of the island's people and have been ever since.

violence.note: Between 18 February and 4 March 1942 Japanese forces screened Singapore's Chinese men and killed those judged hostile. Japanese officers admitted about 5,000 deaths; Singapore Chinese community estimates run to 25,000-50,000, and no full count was ever possible.

toll.note: The low figure comes from Japanese testimony at the 1947 war crimes trial; the high figure from post-war Chinese community surveys. The truth is not recoverable, and the range itself is the honest answer.

warrant.author: The Singapore war crimes trial of 1947, and the post-war Chinese community surveys
warrant.work: Testimony at the Singapore war crimes trial, and the Chinese community’s own surveys of the Sook Ching
warrant.supports: The low figure comes from Japanese testimony at the 1947 war crimes trial; the high figure from post-war Chinese community surveys. The truth is not recoverable, and the range itself is the honest answer.
warrant.check: The trial record is in WO 235 at The National Archives, Kew.
warrant.note: The low figure is what the perpetrators admitted under trial and the high figure is what the survivors counted. The truth is not recoverable, and the range itself is the honest answer.

commonwealth.note: Singapore joined the Commonwealth in its own right two months after separation from Malaysia.

consequences.economicLegacy: A free port with no tariffs for 144 years, Singapore inherited the entrepot trade, the banks and the naval dockyard, and turned the last of them into the world's second-busiest container port.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English common law, English as the language of government and business, and a set of colonial emergency powers — detention without trial under the Internal Security Act — that the independent state kept and used.

peak.populationNote: 1957 census of the Colony of Singapore. About three-quarters of the population was Chinese.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Singapore’s largest recorded population: 1,445,929 people, counted in 1957.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: C. M. Turnbull
evidence.work: A History of Modern Singapore, 1819-2005
evidence.supports: The whole span from the 1819 landing to separation in 1965.

evidence.author: Tim Harper
evidence.work: The End of Empire and the Making of Malaya
evidence.supports: The post-war politics of Singapore and Malaya, the Emergency and the merger debate.

evidence.author: Lee Kuan Yew
evidence.work: The Singapore Story: Memoirs of Lee Kuan Yew
evidence.supports: The merger negotiations and the separation of 1965, from the point of view of the man who led them.

pedagogy.hook: Singapore is the only country in modern history to become independent against its will. It was thrown out of Malaysia in 1965, and its prime minister broke down on live television announcing it.

misconception.belief: Singapore became independent from Britain in 1965.
misconception.correction: British rule over Singapore ended on 16 September 1963, when the island joined Malaysia. The 9 August 1965 separation was a quarrel between Kuala Lumpur and Singapore, not a colonial handover: Malaysia's parliament voted 126 to nil to expel a state whose government it could not control.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Singapore shows that the end of empire was not always a straight line from colony to nation. It also shows what the colonial state left behind: a free port, a common-law system, and a detention-without-trial law that the independent government used on its own opposition within months of taking office.

territories.name: Malacca
territories.formalName: Settlement of Malacca

namesOverTime.name: Melaka

from.note: The traditional founding date of the sultanate under Parameswara; chronicles and archaeology give slightly different dates.

namesOverTime.note: The Malacca Sultanate was the dominant power of the Straits until the Portuguese took the city in 1511.

geoCoverage.label: British occupation of Dutch Malacca
British Malacca
geoCoverage.change: The Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 gave Malacca to Britain permanently in exchange for Bencoolen in Sumatra. Dutch officials handed the town over in 1825.

acquisitions.how: A British squadron took Malacca from its Dutch garrison without a fight, on the authority of the Kew Letters — orders written in England by the exiled Dutch Stadtholder William V telling Dutch governors to admit British troops rather than let the French have their colonies.

counterparties.name: The Dutch East India Company and the Batavian Republic
counterparties.lost: The Netherlands lost the fortress that had controlled the Straits since 1641, and lost it to an ally acting on the orders of its own deposed head of state.
counterparties.note: The Dutch had themselves taken Malacca from Portugal in 1641 after a siege; Portugal had taken it from the Malacca Sultanate in 1511.

instrument.name: The Kew Letters
instrument.note: Not a treaty between states but instructions from a refugee prince at Kew, which Britain used to occupy Dutch colonies from Ceylon to the Moluccas.

acquisitions.how: Britain and the Netherlands swapped colonies in London: the Dutch gave up Malacca and every claim north of the Singapore Strait, and Britain gave up Bencoolen and every claim on Sumatra.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of the Netherlands
counterparties.lost: Malacca and all Dutch claims on the Malay Peninsula, traded for a free hand in Sumatra and the recognition of Dutch power over the archipelago south of the Straits.

counterparties.name: The Johor-Riau Sultanate
counterparties.lost: One Malay maritime state was cut in two by a line drawn in London between people who had never seen it: the peninsula and Singapore to Britain, the Riau-Lingga islands to the Dutch.
counterparties.note: That line is, with small changes, the modern Malaysia-Indonesia border.

instrument.name: Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 (Treaty of London)
instrument.note: Neither Malay ruler affected by the treaty was consulted, or informed until afterwards.

people.name: George Canning
people.role: British Foreign Secretary who authorised the exchange

people.name: Stamford Raffles
people.role: Lieutenant-Governor of Bencoolen; his founding of Singapore in 1819 forced the negotiation

statusPeriods.label: Wartime occupation of a Dutch colony
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British officers ran the town under Company orders from Penang, holding it in trust until the war with France ended, and handed it back to Dutch officials in 1818.
statusPeriods.note: In 1807 the Company ordered the great Portuguese fortress of A Famosa demolished so that Malacca could never rival Penang. Stamford Raffles, then a young secretary at Penang, argued the town was worth keeping. The Porta de Santiago gate survived; the rest did not.

statusPeriods.label: East India Company settlement
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Malacca became one of the three Straits Settlements in 1826, governed by the East India Company from Penang and then Singapore, and left to decline as trade moved to its rivals.
statusPeriods.gapReason: Malacca was Dutch again between September 1818 and 1825. Britain returned it under the 1814 Convention of London and got it back permanently only through the 1824 exchange.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony, Straits Settlements
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Crown replaced the Company in 1858 and the Colonial Office took over in 1867; Malacca was run by a Resident Councillor answering to the Governor in Singapore.

statusPeriods.label: Japanese occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Japanese forces took Malacca on 15 January 1942 as they drove down the peninsula, and ran it through a military administration until the surrender.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Enemy occupation: British authority was zero. Modelled as 'occupied' with degree 0 per the data model's rule.

statusPeriods.label: Settlement of the Federation of Malaya
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British military government to April 1946, then a settlement of the Malayan Union and from 1948 of the Federation of Malaya, under the High Commissioner in Kuala Lumpur.
statusPeriods.franchise: Federal elections in 1955 on a citizenship-based register; before that, nobody voted.
statusPeriods.note: On 20 February 1956 Tunku Abdul Rahman announced at the Padang Bandar Hilir in Malacca that Malaya would be independent within two years. Malacca has called itself the historic city of independence ever since.

departures.how: Malacca became independent as a state of the Federation of Malaya, 446 years after Portuguese guns ended the sultanate and 162 years after a British squadron first sailed in.

led.name: Tunku Abdul Rahman
led.role: Chief Minister who chose Malacca for the 1956 independence announcement

led.name: Tan Cheng Lock
led.role: Malacca-born leader of the Malayan Chinese Association; built the Alliance with UMNO that made independence negotiable

cost.note: Nobody died in Malacca at independence. The Emergency, still running in 1957, had killed thousands elsewhere in Malaya.

departures.borders: No border moved. A settlement governed from Singapore for 130 years became a state governed from Kuala Lumpur, keeping the boundaries the Dutch had drawn.

consequences.economicLegacy: Malacca's harbour silted and its trade went to Penang and Singapore; by 1900 it exported little but tapioca and rubber, and it survives today largely on the tourism of its own ruins.
consequences.languageAndLaw: Four European legal orders left their marks in 300 years: Portuguese Catholic parishes, Dutch land titles, English common law, and a Kristang creole still spoken by a few hundred people.

areaWarrant.author: This atlas, measuring the ground it draws
areaWarrant.work: app/data/geo/units.index.json — Natural Earth 1:10m admin boundaries, measured on a sphere of radius 6,371 km by tools/build-geo.js
areaWarrant.supports: Malacca’s greatest extent, 1,657 km² in 1957: the 1 map unit this atlas draws it holding that year measure 1,693 km², within 2.2% of it.
areaWarrant.check: Open the atlas at that year and select this territory: the outline you see IS the figure. Its units are listed under `geoCoverage` in the shard and measured in app/data/geo/units.index.json, from Natural Earth 1:10m boundaries — public domain, naturalearthdata.com.
areaWarrant.note: A modern outline measured to check an older figure. It confirms the size and the shape to within a twentieth; it is not the surveyed border of that year, and no colonial border was ever surveyed to that precision anyway.

evidence.author: Barbara Watson Andaya and Leonard Y. Andaya
evidence.work: A History of Malaysia
evidence.supports: Malacca from sultanate to Portuguese, Dutch and British rule.

evidence.author: Nicholas Tarling
evidence.work: Anglo-Dutch Rivalry in the Malay World, 1780-1824
evidence.supports: The 1795 occupation, the 1818 return and the 1824 exchange.

pedagogy.hook: In 1807 the British blew up Malacca's Portuguese fortress so it could never compete with Penang. A young clerk called Stamford Raffles talked them out of finishing the job; one gate still stands.

misconception.belief: European empires in Asia replaced each other neatly, one after another.
misconception.correction: Malacca changed hands five times in 450 years and twice in twenty-nine: Malay sultanate to Portugal in 1511, to the Dutch in 1641, to Britain in 1795, back to the Dutch in 1818, and to Britain again in 1825 — that last time as a swap for a pepper port in Sumatra, agreed in London by men who never asked anyone who lived there.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Malacca shows empire as bookkeeping. The 1824 treaty exchanged one town for another and, in doing so, drew the line that still separates Malaysia from Indonesia and split the Johor-Riau sultanate in half.

territories.name: Bencoolen
territories.formalName: The British Settlement of Fort Marlborough, Bencoolen, West Sumatra

from.note: The Malay name of the coast and its principal river; the English spelling 'Bencoolen' is a corruption of it.

modernSuccessors.name: Indonesia (province of Bengkulu)
modernSuccessors.note: Dutch from 1825, Japanese from 1942, Indonesian after the revolution of 1945-49.

geoCoverage.label: Fort Marlborough and the pepper coast
With the captured Dutch posts, including Padang
geoCoverage.change: British forces took the Dutch west-coast settlements, Padang above all, in 1795 and held them until 1819. Only a string of coastal forts was ever occupied, never the interior.

geoCoverage.label: Bencoolen alone again
geoCoverage.change: Padang and the other captured Dutch posts were returned to the Netherlands in 1819 under the 1814 Convention of London.

acquisitions.how: Thrown out of Banten by the Dutch in 1682, the East India Company asked the chiefs of the Bengkulu coast for a site to buy pepper and built Fort York on a malarial river mouth in 1685.

counterparties.name: The chiefs of Bengkulu, Silebar and the Sumatran pepper districts
counterparties.lost: They kept their land and their rulers but lost control of the price of pepper, and were pushed into compulsory planting quotas that the Company enforced through its own appointed headmen.
counterparties.note: Bencoolen was never conquered. It was a lease that hardened into a claim, and the Company's authority rarely reached more than a few miles inland.

people.name: Ralph Ord and Benjamin Bloome
people.role: Company agents who negotiated the first site at Bengkulu in 1685

people.name: Stamford Raffles
people.role: Lieutenant-Governor 1818-24; abolished the compulsory pepper system, banned slavery in the settlement, and founded Singapore from here

contested.note: Company records give 1685 for the first agreement and 1685-86 for the building of Fort York; the settlement moved to Fort Marlborough, three miles away, in 1714 after the first fort proved unliveable.

evidence.author: John Bastin
evidence.work: The British in West Sumatra (1685-1825)
evidence.supports: The founding of Bencoolen, the pepper system and the settlement's finances.

to.note: There is no single moment when the Company stopped asking and started ordering; historians place the shift in the mid-eighteenth century, when the pepper quotas became compulsory.

statusPeriods.label: Company pepper factory
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A handful of Company servants held a fort and bought pepper from Sumatran growers, on terms they negotiated rather than imposed, and died of fever at a rate that made Bencoolen a punishment posting.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Fort Marlborough, under Fort St George in Madras

from.note: See the note on the previous period: the change was gradual.

statusPeriods.label: Company residency on the pepper coast
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Company governed through appointed Sumatran headmen, set compulsory pepper quotas, and by 1800 was losing money on the settlement every single year.
statusPeriods.note: Raffles governed here from 1818 to 1824 and hated it: he called Bencoolen the most wretched place he had ever seen, abolished the forced pepper deliveries, and looked north for a better port. He found Singapore.

departures.how: Britain handed Bencoolen to the Netherlands under the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824, in exchange for Malacca and a free hand on the Malay Peninsula, and the Union flag came down over Fort Marlborough in April 1825.

led.name: George Canning
led.role: British Foreign Secretary; approved trading a 139-year-old settlement for a better position in the Straits

led.name: Stamford Raffles
led.role: the settlement's last effective British governor, whose founding of Singapore made Bencoolen expendable

cost.note: Nobody was killed in the handover. The Sumatrans of the pepper districts were not asked and were not told until British officials began packing; within a decade the Dutch were fighting the Padri War in the highlands behind them.

departures.borders: The 1824 treaty drew a line through the Straits of Malacca: everything south and west Dutch, everything north and east British. That line is the Malaysia-Indonesia border today.

populationTransfer.note: The Company shipped convicts from Bengal and Madras to build Fort Marlborough and clear pepper gardens; Bencoolen was a penal station as well as a trading post, and enslaved people were bought and held there until Raffles banned the practice in 1818.

consequences.economicLegacy: Bencoolen lost money for the East India Company in almost every year of its existence — the clearest single example in the empire of a colony held for prestige and habit rather than profit.
consequences.borderLegacy: By trading Bencoolen away, Britain accepted that Sumatra was Dutch. The result was the modern division of the Malay world into two countries speaking one language.

evidence.author: John Bastin
evidence.work: The British in West Sumatra (1685-1825)
evidence.supports: The settlement's founding, administration, finances and transfer.

evidence.author: Nicholas Tarling
evidence.work: Anglo-Dutch Rivalry in the Malay World, 1780-1824
evidence.supports: The 1795 seizures of Dutch posts and the 1824 exchange.

contested.note: The reach of British authority inland from Bencoolen is genuinely unclear: the Company claimed a long coastline and a pepper monopoly, but administered only a few forts and their immediate districts. The map shows the claim, not the control, which is why the whole area is drawn as partial.

pedagogy.hook: Britain held a piece of Sumatra for 139 years, lost money on it almost every year, and finally swapped it for Malacca — a trade that created the border between Malaysia and Indonesia.

misconception.belief: The British empire took territory because territory was profitable.
misconception.correction: Bencoolen ran at a loss for well over a century and everyone in London knew it. It survived because abandoning a post looked like weakness, and it ended only when Raffles found a better harbour at Singapore and made it possible to trade Bencoolen away.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: This is where Raffles was working when he sailed north and founded Singapore. The failed pepper colony paid for the idea that replaced it, and its disposal in 1824 fixed the map of maritime South-East Asia for good.

territories.name: British Java
territories.formalName: The British occupation of Java and its dependencies

from.note: The island's own name, used in Javanese and Malay long before any European map.

modernSuccessors.name: Indonesia
modernSuccessors.note: Independence proclaimed 17 August 1945; the Netherlands recognised it on 27 December 1949 after four years of war.

geoCoverage.label: Java under Lieutenant-Governor Raffles

acquisitions.how: An East India Company expedition of about 11,000 men landed near Batavia in August 1811 and beat the Franco-Dutch army of Governor-General Jan Willem Janssens, who surrendered at Salatiga on 18 September.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of Holland under Napoleonic France
counterparties.lost: The Netherlands, then a French satellite, lost its richest colony for five years, along with its coffee monopoly and its army in the East.

counterparties.name: The Javanese courts of Yogyakarta and Surakarta
counterparties.lost: Yogyakarta lost its independence of action, its treasury and its library: British troops stormed the kraton in June 1812, deposed Sultan Hamengkubuwono II and carried off the palace archive, much of which is still in London.
counterparties.note: The sacking is remembered in Java as the Geger Sepehi, the 'sepoy uprising', after the Indian soldiers who did most of the fighting.

people.name: Gilbert Elliot, Lord Minto
people.role: Governor-General of India; ordered and accompanied the invasion

people.name: Stamford Raffles
people.role: Lieutenant-Governor of Java 1811-16; imposed a land-rent system and ordered the assault on Yogyakarta

people.name: Jan Willem Janssens
people.role: Franco-Dutch Governor-General who surrendered the island

people.name: Sultan Hamengkubuwono II
people.role: ruler of Yogyakarta, deposed and exiled to Penang after the storming of his palace

people.name: Prince Diponegoro
people.role: grandson of the deposed Sultan; witnessed the sack as a young man and led the Java War against the Dutch in 1825-30

acquisitions.resistance: Yogyakarta resisted and was stormed on 20 June 1812; Palembang's Sultan Mahmud Badaruddin II was deposed after massacring the Dutch garrison, and the Company took Bangka from him as a prize.

evidence.author: Peter Carey
evidence.work: The Power of Prophecy: Prince Dipanagara and the End of the Old Order in Java, 1785-1855
evidence.supports: The British invasion, the storming of the Yogyakarta kraton and its consequences for Javanese politics.

statusPeriods.label: East India Company occupation government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Raffles governed from Batavia as Lieutenant-Governor for the East India Company, replaced the Dutch forced-delivery system with a cash land rent, and answered to Calcutta rather than to London.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Batavia, under Fort William in Calcutta
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. Javanese rulers kept their thrones on British terms; two of them lost them.
statusPeriods.note: Raffles used the five years to survey the island, dig at Borobudur and write The History of Java (1817). His land-rent scheme raised less money than the Dutch system it replaced and was largely abandoned after 1816.

departures.how: Britain handed Java back to the restored Kingdom of the Netherlands under the Convention of London of 1814, as part of building a strong Dutch state on France's northern flank; the transfer was completed in August 1816.

led.name: Robert Stewart, Viscount Castlereagh
led.role: British Foreign Secretary; traded the colony back to strengthen the Netherlands against France

led.name: John Fendall
led.role: the last British Lieutenant-Governor, who handed Java over in August 1816

cost.note: The handover itself killed nobody, but it returned Java to a Dutch administration that within nine years faced the Java War of 1825-30, in which an estimated 200,000 Javanese and 15,000 government soldiers died. Both figures are Dutch reconstructions with wide margins.

departures.borders: No border changed. Britain gave back an island it had beaten France for, and kept the trading rights it wanted instead — a preference for commerce over territory that shaped the whole region.

violence.note: The storming of the Yogyakarta kraton on 20 June 1812 was the first time a European army had taken a Javanese royal palace; the court's treasury and manuscript library were carried off, and much of the library is now in the British Library and the Royal Asiatic Society.

consequences.economicLegacy: Raffles's land-rent system was meant to turn Javanese peasants into taxpaying smallholders. It failed, and the Dutch replaced it in 1830 with the Cultivation System, a far harsher regime of compulsory export crops.
consequences.borderLegacy: Britain's decision to hand Java back settled the archipelago on the Dutch, and pushed British ambition north to the Straits — where Raffles founded Singapore three years later.

peak.populationNote: Raffles's own 1815 census of Java gave about 4.6 million; modern demographers think it undercounted, perhaps badly. It remains the first population count ever attempted for the island.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: British Java’s largest recorded population: 4,600,000 people, counted in 1815.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Peter Carey
evidence.work: The Power of Prophecy: Prince Dipanagara and the End of the Old Order in Java, 1785-1855
evidence.supports: The invasion, the sack of Yogyakarta and the Javanese consequences.

evidence.author: Tim Hannigan
evidence.work: Raffles and the British Invasion of Java
evidence.supports: Narrative of the 1811 campaign and Raffles's five-year administration.

pedagogy.hook: For five years Java was British. In 1812 British and Indian troops stormed the Sultan of Yogyakarta's palace and shipped its library to London, where much of it still sits.

misconception.belief: Britain took colonies whenever it could and never gave any back.
misconception.correction: Britain conquered Java in 1811 and returned it to the Dutch in 1816, along with the Moluccas, Sumatra's west coast and the Cape's Indonesian dependencies. It kept Ceylon, the Cape and Malacca instead. The empire traded territory for strategic advantage, and it was quite willing to hand back an island of four million people to build a stronger buffer against France.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Java is the clearest case in the region of empire as chess. It also produced two things that outlasted the occupation: Raffles's search for a British port in the Straits, which became Singapore, and the humiliation of Yogyakarta, which helped set off the Java War of 1825-30.

territories.name: British Moluccas
territories.formalName: The British occupations of Amboyna, Banda and the Spice Islands

geoCoverage.label: First occupation: Amboyna and Banda
Second occupation
geoCoverage.change: The islands were handed back to the Dutch in 1803 under the Peace of Amiens and taken again when war resumed: Amboyna in February 1810, Banda Neira in August.

acquisitions.how: A British squadron under Rear-Admiral Peter Rainier took Amboyna in February 1796 and Banda a month later, seizing the world's only source of nutmeg and cloves from a Dutch garrison cut off from a Netherlands under French control.

counterparties.name: The Dutch East India Company
counterparties.lost: The spice monopoly it had held since the 1620s, and the islands it had depopulated to keep it.
counterparties.note: The Dutch had massacred or deported almost the entire population of the Banda Islands in 1621 to secure the nutmeg trade; the people the British found there in 1796 were largely enslaved workers and their descendants.

counterparties.name: The people of the Banda and Ambon islands
counterparties.lost: Nothing was returned to them: a change of European flag left the nutmeg plantations, and the forced labour that worked them, exactly as they were.

evidence.author: Nicholas Tarling
evidence.work: Anglo-Dutch Rivalry in the Malay World, 1780-1824
evidence.supports: The seizures of 1796 and 1810 and their diplomatic settlement.

acquisitions.how: Britain took the islands a second time after the Peace of Amiens collapsed; in August 1810 Captain Christopher Cole carried the fortress of Banda Neira, held by some 700 defenders, with about 180 men in a night attack.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of Holland under Napoleonic France
counterparties.lost: The spice islands again, this time for seven years, and with them the last leverage the Dutch monopoly had over the European market.

people.name: Christopher Cole
people.role: Royal Navy captain who stormed Banda Neira in August 1810

statusPeriods.label: First wartime occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Royal Navy officers and East India Company agents held the forts and kept the spice plantations running exactly as the Dutch had, using the same overseers and the same forced labour.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Madras, through naval commanders on station

statusPeriods.label: Second wartime occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The islands were run from Java after 1811 as a dependency of Raffles's government, with British Residents at Ambon and Banda.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Batavia, under the British government of Java
statusPeriods.gapReason: The islands were Dutch again between 1803 and 1810, restored under the Peace of Amiens and retaken when the war resumed.
statusPeriods.note: During both occupations the East India Company dug up nutmeg and clove seedlings and shipped them to Penang, Bencoolen and Ceylon, and later to Grenada. The Dutch monopoly, three centuries old, never recovered.

departures.how: Britain returned the Moluccas to the Netherlands under the Convention of London, keeping the nutmeg and clove seedlings it had already smuggled out.

led.name: Robert Stewart, Viscount Castlereagh
led.role: British Foreign Secretary; returned the Dutch colonies as part of the 1814-15 European settlement

led.name: Thomas Matulessy (Pattimura)
led.role: Ambonese former soldier who led the rising against the returning Dutch in May 1817 and was hanged in December

cost.note: Within weeks of the Dutch return, Ambonese villagers rose under Thomas Matulessy, killed the Dutch Resident at Saparua and held out for six months. Matulessy and three others were hanged at Ambon on 16 December 1817. Contemporary Dutch reports of the dead vary and no reliable total exists.

departures.borders: No line moved. The islands went back into the Dutch empire and became Indonesian in 1949; the nutmeg trees Britain took with it made Grenada a spice exporter instead.

consequences.economicLegacy: Britain broke the world's oldest commodity monopoly by theft: nutmeg and clove seedlings taken from Banda and Ambon during these occupations were replanted in Penang, Ceylon and later Grenada, and the price of nutmeg collapsed within a generation.

violence.note: British rule left the Dutch plantation system intact, including the forced labour that worked it, and Ambonese resistance in 1817 was aimed at the returning Dutch, not at the departing British — several rebels said openly that they had preferred the English.

evidence.author: Nicholas Tarling
evidence.work: Anglo-Dutch Rivalry in the Malay World, 1780-1824
evidence.supports: Both occupations, their administration and the 1817 restitution.

evidence.author: Giles Milton
evidence.work: Nathaniel's Nutmeg: How One Man's Courage Changed the Course of History
evidence.supports: The long Anglo-Dutch struggle for the Banda Islands and the nutmeg monopoly.

contested.note: Dates for the two occupations vary by a year in different accounts because the surrender of individual islands, the formal handovers and the arrival of new governors did not coincide. The dates here follow the capture of the main forts at Amboyna and Banda Neira.

pedagogy.hook: In 1810 Christopher Cole took the nutmeg islands with about 180 men — and Britain used its brief hold to smuggle the seedlings out to Penang and Ceylon, wrecking a Dutch monopoly three centuries old.

misconception.belief: Empires competed by conquering territory.
misconception.correction: The most damaging thing Britain did in the Moluccas was not the conquest but the theft of plants. Once nutmeg and cloves grew in Penang, Ceylon and Grenada, holding Banda was worth nothing, and the islands went back to the Dutch in 1817 without a fight.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Spice Islands are the origin of the whole European presence in South-East Asia, and this is how that era ended: not in battle, but when the plants stopped being rare.

territories.name: British Manila
territories.formalName: The British occupation of Manila and Cavite, 1762-1764

modernSuccessors.name: Philippines
modernSuccessors.note: Spanish until 1898, then American until 1946, apart from the Japanese occupation of 1942-45.

geoCoverage.label: Manila and Cavite only
geoCoverage.change: The map draws the whole archipelago because no smaller unit exists. Britain held two towns on Manila Bay and never controlled anything else in the Philippines.

acquisitions.how: An expedition from Madras stormed Manila on 6 October 1762, and the Spanish Archbishop-Governor bought off the sack of the city by promising a ransom of four million Spanish dollars.

counterparties.name: The Spanish Empire
counterparties.lost: Its Asian capital, its Pacific treasure ship the Santisima Trinidad, and the fiction that Manila was defensible; the Seven Years' War cost Spain both Manila and Havana in a single year.

counterparties.name: The Ilocano and Pampangan peoples of Luzon
counterparties.lost: The revolt Diego Silang launched in the confusion, hoping British help would end Spanish tribute, ended with him assassinated and his wife Gabriela hanged; Spanish rule returned harder than before.
counterparties.note: Britain never sent Silang the support he was promised. The Ilocano rising was crushed by Spanish and allied forces while British troops stayed in Manila.

people.name: William Draper
people.role: brigadier-general who commanded the assault on Manila

people.name: Samuel Cornish
people.role: vice-admiral commanding the squadron from Madras

people.name: Manuel Rojo del Rio
people.role: Archbishop and acting Governor of the Philippines; surrendered the city and signed the ransom

people.name: Simon de Anda y Salazar
people.role: Spanish judge who refused the surrender, escaped to Pampanga and ran a resistance government from Bacolor

people.name: Diego Silang
people.role: Ilocano leader who rose against Spain and sought a British alliance; assassinated 28 May 1763

people.name: Gabriela Silang
people.role: continued her husband's revolt after his murder; captured and hanged on 20 September 1763

acquisitions.resistance: Simon de Anda kept a Spanish government alive in Pampanga for the whole occupation, blockading Manila by land, so British authority never extended beyond the reach of its own guns.

evidence.author: Nicholas Tracy
evidence.work: Manila Ransomed: The British Assault on Manila in the Seven Years War
evidence.supports: The assault, the ransom negotiation and the failure to collect it.

statusPeriods.label: East India Company military occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British and sepoy troops held Manila and Cavite under a Company governor while a Spanish government-in-exile at Bacolor blockaded them by land and collected the taxes.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Full British authority inside Manila and Cavite, and none at all outside them. The degree describes the occupied towns, not the archipelago the map has to draw.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Manila, under Fort St George in Madras

departures.how: The Treaty of Paris had already ended the war before the news reached Asia; British troops handed Manila back to Spain in 1764 and sailed away with roughly half a million of the four million dollars they had been promised.

led.name: Dawsonne Drake
led.role: the Company's governor of Manila, who handed the city back and was later censured for profiteering

led.name: Simon de Anda y Salazar
led.role: leader of the Spanish resistance; returned to Manila and became its Governor

cost.money: Of the four million Spanish dollars promised as ransom, roughly half a million was paid. Spain repudiated the rest, and the debt was still being argued about in the nineteenth century.
cost.note: British and sepoy losses in the assault were light; Spanish and Filipino losses in the storming of the city and in the associated revolts are not reliably counted. Diego and Gabriela Silang were both killed, and Ilocano communities suffered heavy reprisals.

departures.borders: No border changed. The Philippines stayed Spanish for another 134 years, and the episode survives mainly as a warning about how thin Spanish power in Asia had become.

instrument.name: Treaty of Paris (1763)
instrument.note: Manila was captured after the peace preliminaries were agreed in Europe but before anyone in Asia knew; Britain had to give it back.

violence.note: The occupation set off two risings that Britain encouraged and then abandoned: Diego Silang's in Ilocos and a Chinese community rising in Manila, both put down by Spanish forces with heavy reprisals against those who had sided with the British.

consequences.economicLegacy: The ransom of Manila became one of the great unpaid debts of the eighteenth century and helped convince the East India Company that raiding Spanish America and Asia was less profitable than taxing Bengal.

territories.name: Macau (British landing, 1808)
territories.formalName: The British occupation of Macau, September to December 1808

modernSuccessors.name: Macao Special Administrative Region, China
modernSuccessors.note: Portuguese-administered from 1557 under Chinese sovereignty, a Portuguese colony from 1887, and Chinese again from 1999.

geoCoverage.label: British troops in the Portuguese settlement

acquisitions.how: Rear-Admiral William O'Brien Drury landed about three hundred troops at Macau to hold it against a French seizure that never came, over the protests of the Portuguese governor and without asking China, which owned the ground.

counterparties.name: The Portuguese settlement of Macau
counterparties.lost: Its neutrality. Portugal had held Macau on Chinese sufferance since 1557, paying ground rent to the Qing, and a British garrison put that arrangement in danger.

counterparties.name: The Qing Empire
counterparties.lost: Nothing, in the end: the Jiaqing Emperor treated the landing as a violation of Chinese soil, suspended the Canton trade until the troops left, and won.
counterparties.note: This is the clearest demonstration that before 1839 China could still dictate terms to Britain, simply by closing the tea trade.

people.name: William O'Brien Drury
people.role: rear-admiral who landed the troops and then had to withdraw them

people.name: The Jiaqing Emperor
people.role: ordered the British out and suspended trade at Canton until they went

acquisitions.resistance: The Portuguese governor refused to cooperate, the Chinese authorities cut off supplies and stopped the tea trade, and the East India Company's Select Committee at Canton begged Drury to leave before the season's cargoes were lost.

evidence.author: Robert Bickers
evidence.work: The Scramble for China: Foreign Devils in the Qing Empire, 1832-1914
evidence.supports: The pre-1839 balance of power at Canton and Macau and the limits of British leverage.

statusPeriods.label: Three months of British troops in Macau
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British marines and sepoys occupied the forts while Portuguese officials went on administering the town and Chinese officials went on refusing to recognise that anything had changed.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: British soldiers held the forts but never displaced the Portuguese administration or the Qing authorities above it, so this was far short of the full sovereignty 'occupied' usually implies.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: the flagship, and the Company's Select Committee at Canton

departures.how: Britain withdrew its troops in December 1808 because the Jiaqing Emperor stopped the Canton trade until they left, and the tea was worth more than the harbour.

led.name: William O'Brien Drury
led.role: withdrew the force he had landed, on the Company's insistence

led.name: Wu Xiongguang
led.role: Viceroy of Liangguang, who cut off trade and supplies until the British left

cost.note: No fighting and no recorded deaths. The cost was commercial: a season of the Canton trade was disrupted, which was precisely the point.

departures.borders: No border moved. The episode mattered because of what it proved: in 1808 China could still expel a British force by economic pressure alone. Thirty-one years later, at Hong Kong, it could not.

consequences.economicLegacy: The failure at Macau taught British merchants that they needed a base outside Chinese jurisdiction. Thirty-three years later they took one, sixty kilometres east, and called it Hong Kong.

evidence.author: Austin Coates
evidence.work: A Macao Narrative
evidence.supports: The 1808 landing, the Portuguese reaction and the withdrawal.

evidence.author: Robert Bickers
evidence.work: The Scramble for China: Foreign Devils in the Qing Empire, 1832-1914
evidence.supports: British commercial dependence on Canton and the limits of British power before 1839.

contested.note: The exact dates of landing and withdrawal differ by a few days between British naval records, Portuguese Macau records and Qing memorials. The size of the force is given variously as 300 to 700 men.

pedagogy.hook: Thirty-three years before Hong Kong, Britain seized Macau to keep it from Napoleon — and sailed away three months later because the Chinese emperor simply stopped selling tea.

misconception.belief: Britain could take what it wanted in Asia whenever it chose.
misconception.correction: In 1808 the Qing state expelled a British force from the Pearl River without firing a shot, by suspending the Canton trade. British power in China was not built on guns until the 1840s; before that it depended on Chinese permission, and everyone involved knew it.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: This is the control experiment for the Opium Wars. The same British interests, the same coast, thirty years apart — and the difference in outcome is the difference steam warships and a willingness to bombard cities made.

territories.name: Federation of Malaya
territories.formalName: The Federation of Malaya (Persekutuan Tanah Melayu)

namesOverTime.name: Malayan Union
namesOverTime.note: A single British colony that abolished the sultans' sovereignty and gave equal citizenship to all races. Malay opposition killed it in 22 months.

namesOverTime.name: Persekutuan Tanah Melayu
namesOverTime.note: Literally 'the federation of the Malay lands' — a name that carried the political argument the Malayan Union had lost.

modernSuccessors.name: Malaysia
modernSuccessors.note: The Federation of Malaya became Malaysia in 1963 by adding Singapore, Sarawak and North Borneo; Singapore left in 1965.

geoCoverage.label: Nine Malay states and two settlements
geoCoverage.change: Britain merged the four federated states, the five unfederated states and the settlements of Penang and Malacca into one government, and deliberately left Singapore out.

acquisitions.how: Britain merged nine protected Malay states and two settlements into one colony, the Malayan Union, taking the sultans' sovereignty outright on signatures Harold MacMichael had collected in six weeks, some under threat of non-recognition.

counterparties.name: The nine Malay rulers
counterparties.lost: Sovereignty itself. The treaties of 1874 to 1919 had always left the sultans as rulers advised by Britain; the Malayan Union made them British subjects with religious duties and nothing else.
counterparties.note: MacMichael visited each ruler between October and December 1945, sometimes hinting that a ruler who had cooperated with the Japanese might not be recognised if he refused.

counterparties.name: The Chinese and Indian residents of Malaya
counterparties.lost: They gained on paper and lost in practice: the Union offered them equal citizenship by birth, and when Malay protest destroyed the Union in 1948 the replacement made citizenship far harder for them to obtain.
counterparties.note: Under the 1948 Federation agreement, most Malayan-born Chinese did not automatically qualify as citizens.

people.name: Harold MacMichael
people.role: special envoy who obtained the rulers' signatures in six weeks

people.name: Onn Jaafar
people.role: Johor official who organised the mass Malay protest and founded UMNO on 11 May 1946

people.name: Edward Gent
people.role: the only Governor of the Malayan Union; the sultans boycotted his installation

acquisitions.resistance: Malays turned out in tens of thousands in white mourning headbands, the sultans boycotted the Governor's installation, and two former Governors of Malaya attacked the scheme in the House of Lords. Britain abandoned it in under two years.

evidence.author: Tim Harper
evidence.work: The End of Empire and the Making of Malaya
evidence.supports: The MacMichael mission, the Malayan Union crisis and the 1948 Federation settlement.

statusPeriods.label: Malayan Union: a single British colony
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British Governor ruled the whole peninsula outside Singapore with an appointed council; the sultans kept only religious authority, and Malayan citizenship was open to anyone born there.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kuala Lumpur, under the Colonial Office
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted, but the Union's citizenship rules would have given the vote, in time, to Chinese and Indian Malayans on equal terms with Malays.

statusPeriods.label: Federation of Malaya under a High Commissioner
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The sultans got their sovereignty back and Britain kept the power: a British High Commissioner presided over a federal government of nine protected states and two settlements, and from June 1948 ran it under Emergency regulations.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Nominally a set of protected states, but under Emergency regulations from 1948 the High Commissioner could detain, deport, impose curfews and resettle whole villages, so British power was far greater than the protectorate label suggests.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kuala Lumpur, under the Colonial Office
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted federally until 1955. Citizenship rules excluded most Malayan-born Chinese, which was the point of the change from the Union.
statusPeriods.note: The Emergency was declared on 18 June 1948. Under the Briggs Plan from 1950 about 500,000 rural people, most of them Chinese, were moved into 450 fenced and guarded New Villages.

statusPeriods.label: Elected government under Tunku Abdul Rahman
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Alliance won 51 of 52 elected seats in July 1955 and Tunku Abdul Rahman became Chief Minister; Britain kept defence, external affairs and internal security while the independence terms were negotiated in London.
statusPeriods.franchise: About 1.28 million people were registered for the 1955 election, of whom the great majority were Malays because of the citizenship rules.
statusPeriods.note: The Tunku met Chin Peng at Baling in December 1955 and offered an amnesty but refused to legalise the Malayan Communist Party. The talks failed and the Emergency ran until 1960.

departures.how: Britain handed over to an elected Malayan government at midnight on 31 August 1957, after four years of talks, an armed rebellion it had largely defeated, and a bargain between Malay, Chinese and Indian parties that traded citizenship for special Malay rights.

led.name: Tan Cheng Lock

led.name: V. T. Sambanthan
led.role: leader of the Malayan Indian Congress and the third partner in the Alliance

led.name: Chin Peng
led.role: secretary-general of the Malayan Communist Party, which fought Britain from 1948 and was excluded from the settlement

led.name: Gerald Templer
led.role: High Commissioner 1952-54; combined resettlement, food control and the promise of independence into the strategy that broke the insurgency

cost.note: Malayan government figures for the Emergency of 1948-60: 6,710 insurgents, 1,346 Malayan police and soldiers, 519 Commonwealth troops and 2,478 civilians killed, with 810 civilians missing. warrant.work: The Malayan Emergency: Revolution and Counterinsurgency at the End of Empire
warrant.supports: Emergency casualty figures, the resettlement programme and the link between counter-insurgency and the timing of independence.

departures.borders: The federation took the peninsula's existing state boundaries and Britain's 1909 line with Thailand, and left out Singapore — a decision made in 1946 for demographic reasons that produced the separate country next door.

instrument.name: Federation of Malaya Independence Act 1957
instrument.note: Royal assent 31 July 1957; independence took effect at midnight on 31 August 1957.

evidence.author: Karl Hack
evidence.work: The Malayan Emergency: Revolution and Counterinsurgency at the End of Empire
evidence.supports: Emergency casualty figures, the resettlement programme and the link between counter-insurgency and the timing of independence.

violence.note: Britain fought a twelve-year counter-insurgency here and won it, using mass resettlement, food denial, deportation of about 30,000 people to China, collective punishment and the death penalty for carrying arms.

toll.note: Official Malayan totals: 6,710 insurgents, 1,865 security forces and 2,478 civilians killed, plus 810 civilians missing. Deaths among resettled villagers from disease and hunger are not in any official count.

populationTransfer.note: The Briggs Plan of 1950 moved roughly half a million rural people, overwhelmingly Chinese, behind wire into New Villages under curfew and food rationing; around 30,000 more were deported to China.

commonwealth.note: Malaya, and then Malaysia, joined the Commonwealth at independence with its own elected king as head of state.

consequences.economicLegacy: Malayan rubber and tin earned more United States dollars in the late 1940s than any British export, which is why a bankrupt Britain fought so hard and so long to keep the country.
consequences.languageAndLaw: The 1957 constitution kept the sultans, made Islam the religion of the federation, made Malay the national language and wrote in special positions for Malays under Article 153 — the bargain that bought independence and the argument that has run ever since.
consequences.borderLegacy: Independence came without Singapore, because Britain had separated it in 1946 to keep Malaya's Malay majority. The consequences of that arithmetic ran through 1963 and 1965 and are still visible on the map.

pedagogy.hook: Britain fought a twelve-year war here and won it — and then handed the country over anyway, three years before the shooting stopped.

misconception.belief: Britain left its colonies when nationalists defeated it, or when it decided to be generous.
misconception.correction: In Malaya Britain beat the insurgency and left anyway. Independence was the weapon: promising it to Tunku Abdul Rahman's Alliance stripped the Malayan Communist Party of its anti-colonial argument. The country was worth too much in dollar earnings to lose, and the surest way to keep it in the Western camp was to give it up.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Malaya is the single best test of what 'decolonisation' meant.
