territories.name: Federated Malay States
territories.formalName: The Federated Malay States (Perak, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan and Pahang)

geoCoverage.label: Four states, one Resident-General, one capital

acquisitions.how: Britain federated four states it already controlled, put a Resident-General over their four Residents in Kuala Lumpur, and pooled their revenues — a centralisation the sultans agreed to without understanding how much further it would go.

counterparties.name: The Sultans of Perak, Selangor and Pahang and the Yang di-Pertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan
counterparties.lost: What remained of their separate identity in government: after 1896 their revenues went into a common purse and the decisions were made by an official in another state's capital.
counterparties.note: The rulers protested at the Durbars of 1897 and 1903 that they had been reduced to figureheads. Sultan Idris of Perak said in 1903 that the federation had taken from the rulers the very authority the treaties had promised to protect.

instrument.name: Treaty of Federation, 1895
instrument.note: Signed by the four rulers in 1895 and brought into effect on 1 July 1896.

people.name: Frank Swettenham
people.role: architect of the federation and its first Resident-General

people.name: Sultan Idris Murshidul Azzam Shah
people.role: Sultan of Perak; the leading critic of federation among the rulers

statusPeriods.label: Federation under a Resident-General
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Resident-General, renamed Chief Secretary in 1911, ran four states from Kuala Lumpur through a professional civil service; the sultans sat in a Federal Council from 1909 and could be outvoted in it.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kuala Lumpur, under the High Commissioner at Singapore
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. The Federal Council of 1909 had British officials, the four rulers and a handful of nominated unofficial members, and the rulers stopped attending after 1927.
statusPeriods.note: From the 1920s London tried to decentralise power back to the states, partly to make the federation attractive to Johor and the northern states. It never worked: the civil service in Kuala Lumpur was too useful to dismantle.

statusPeriods.label: Japanese occupation of Malaya
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Japan invaded on 8 December 1941 and had taken all four states within six weeks, running Malaya from Singapore as a military territory.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Enemy occupation; British authority was zero across all four states.

statusPeriods.label: British Military Administration
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Army officers governed the four states for seven months while London prepared to abolish the federation and the sultans' sovereignty together.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kuala Lumpur, under South East Asia Command

departures.how: The federation was dissolved into the Malayan Union, a single British colony that took the sultans' sovereignty outright; nobody became independent, and the arrangement collapsed within two years under Malay protest.

becomes.name: Malayan Union, then the Federation of Malaya

led.name: Harold MacMichael
led.role: envoy who obtained the sultans' signatures to the Union in six weeks, several under threat of non-recognition

led.name: Onn Jaafar

cost.note: No one died. The cost was political: Britain's attempt to impose equal citizenship on Malaya without consent created the mass Malay party, UMNO, that would negotiate independence against it eleven years later.

consequences.borderLegacy: The federation built the roads, railway and civil service that made a single Malayan state thinkable; independent Malaysia inherited the machinery almost intact.
consequences.languageAndLaw: The Malay sultans' constitutional position — sovereign in religion and custom, advised in everything else — survived the federation, the Union and independence, and is written into Malaysia's constitution.

territories.name: Perak
territories.formalName: The Protected State of Perak

geoCoverage.label: The sultanate, including the Dindings
geoCoverage.change: The drawn shape is the modern state. The Dindings and Pangkor, ceded to Britain in 1874 and administered from Singapore until 1935, cannot be separated from it.

acquisitions.how: Governor Andrew Clarke summoned the rival claimants to Perak's throne aboard a ship off Pangkor, recognised Raja Abdullah as Sultan, and required him in return to accept a British Resident whose advice must be taken on everything except Malay religion and custom.

counterparties.name: The Sultanate of Perak
counterparties.lost: Its independence and its revenues: the Sultan kept his throne and his title, and lost control of taxation, appointments, justice and the tin trade to a British official living beside him.
counterparties.note: The words 'except those touching Malay religion and custom' became the formula for the whole British position in Malaya and are still the shape of Malaysian federalism.

counterparties.name: The Ghee Hin and Hai San Chinese mining societies
counterparties.lost: Their war over the Larut tin fields was ended by British arbitration, and their leaders lost the private armies that had made them the real power in the mining districts.

people.name: Andrew Clarke
people.role: Governor of the Straits Settlements who forced the settlement, exceeding his instructions from London

people.name: Sultan Abdullah Muhammad Shah II
people.role: claimant installed by Britain in exchange for accepting a Resident; exiled to the Seychelles in 1877

people.name: Raja Ismail
people.role: the rival claimant, recognised by many Perak chiefs, who was pushed aside by the British choice

acquisitions.resistance: Perak's chiefs had not agreed to the Engagement and never accepted it; within twenty-two months they had killed the Resident and Britain had to fight a war to impose the terms.

evidence.author: Emily Sadka
evidence.work: The Protected Malay States, 1874-1895
evidence.supports: The Pangkor Engagement and the working of the residential system.

statusPeriods.label: British Resident at the Sultan's court
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British Resident 'advised' the Sultan, and after 1876 that advice was obeyed: the Resident controlled revenue, appointed district officers and ran the courts, while the Sultan kept religion, custom and a salary.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kuala Kangsar and Taiping, under the Governor at Singapore
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. A State Council of the Sultan, chiefs, the Resident and one or two Chinese leaders met to register decisions already made.
statusPeriods.note: The system nearly failed at once. J. W. W. Birch, the first Resident, tried to abolish debt-slavery and collect taxes directly, and was killed at Pasir Salak on 2 November 1875.

statusPeriods.label: Federated Malay State
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Perak's Resident now answered to a Resident-General in Kuala Lumpur, and the state's tin revenues were pooled to build federal railways and roads; the Sultan's council mattered less every decade.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kuala Lumpur, under the High Commissioner at Singapore
statusPeriods.note: Perak's Kinta valley became the largest tin-producing district in the world; the workforce was overwhelmingly Chinese, recruited through labour brokers and paid through the same opium and gambling farms that funded the state.

statusPeriods.label: Japanese occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Japanese forces overran Perak within a fortnight of landing in Malaya and ran it through a military administration; the anti-Japanese guerrillas of the MPAJA, mostly Chinese and communist-led, took to the Perak jungle and were armed by Britain.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Enemy occupation; British authority was zero. Modelled per the data model's rule.

statusPeriods.label: Malayan Union, then Federation of Malaya
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain first abolished the Sultan's sovereignty in the Malayan Union of 1946, then restored it under the Federation of Malaya in 1948 after Malay protest, and fought the Emergency from Perak, where it began.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kuala Lumpur, under the High Commissioner
statusPeriods.franchise: State elections from 1954 and federal elections in 1955, on a register limited to citizens.
statusPeriods.note: The Emergency was declared on 16 June 1948 after three European planters were shot at Sungai Siput in Perak. It ran for twelve years.

departures.how: Perak became independent as one of eleven states of the Federation of Malaya, its Sultan restored to full sovereignty and made one of the nine rulers who elect Malaysia's king.

led.name: Tunku Abdul Rahman
led.role: Chief Minister of Malaya and leader of the independence delegation

led.name: Sultan Yussuf Izzuddin Shah
led.role: Sultan of Perak at independence; his family's throne had been under British direction for 83 years

consequences.languageAndLaw: The Pangkor formula — British control of everything except Malay religion and custom — is the ancestor of the division of powers between federal and state governments in Malaysia today.

territories.formalName: The Protected State of Selangor

modernSuccessors.name: Malaysia (state of Selangor, and the federal territory of Kuala Lumpur)
modernSuccessors.note: Kuala Lumpur was carved out of Selangor as a federal territory in 1974.

geoCoverage.label: The sultanate and the Klang valley

acquisitions.how: After eight years of civil war over the Klang valley tin mines, Sultan Abdul Samad accepted a British Resident on the Perak model, and Britain became the arbiter of a conflict it had helped to prolong by backing one side's arms supply.

counterparties.lost: Control of its revenue, its courts and its appointments; Sultan Abdul Samad kept his throne and a pension and withdrew from public business almost entirely.

counterparties.name: Raja Mahadi and the Selangor chiefs
counterparties.lost: The war for the Klang valley, and with it any chance of a Malay settlement of the succession without European arbitration.
counterparties.note: Raja Mahadi had taken Klang in 1866 from Raja Abdullah; the Sultan's son-in-law Tengku Kudin brought in outside forces and, in the end, the British.

geoCoverage.label: Sungai Ujong first, then the whole confederation
geoCoverage.change: Britain took the small states one at a time from 1874; the nine were finally reassembled as a single state under one ruler in 1895.

acquisitions.how: The Dato Klana of Sungai Ujong, one of the nine small Minangkabau states behind Malacca, accepted a British Resident to settle a tin-revenue quarrel with a rival chief, and Britain took the other eight over the following twenty years.

counterparties.name: The nine states of Negeri Sembilan
counterparties.lost: A confederation of small Minangkabau chiefdoms with an elected paramount ruler and matrilineal land law lost its independence piece by piece, and was reassembled in 1895 in the shape Britain found convenient.

counterparties.name: The Dato Bandar of Sungai Ujong

territories.name: Pahang
territories.formalName: The Protected State of Pahang

geoCoverage.label: The largest state on the peninsula

acquisitions.how: Sultan Ahmad had resisted a Resident for years; when a Chinese British subject was killed at Pekan in 1888 the Governor used the death as the lever, and a Resident was installed within months.

counterparties.name: The Sultanate of Pahang
counterparties.lost: The Sultan lost the revenues and the appointments that had let him reward his chiefs, and the chiefs lost the districts they had held by custom to salaried officials chosen by the Resident.
counterparties.note: It was that loss, more than the Sultan's, that started the war of 1891.

instrument.note: Sultan Ahmad had signed a lesser treaty in 1887 accepting a British Agent; the 1888 agreement upgraded that to a full Resident.

people.name: Sultan Ahmad al-Muadzam Shah
people.role: ruler who resisted a Resident for a decade and then accepted one under pressure

people.name: Hugh Clifford
people.role: British officer who negotiated in Pahang and later hunted its rebels through the jungle

acquisitions.resistance: The chiefs displaced by the new district system rose in December 1891 under Dato Bahaman, Mat Kilau and Tok Gajah, and fought a guerrilla war along the Pahang river for four years.

statusPeriods.label: British Resident, and a war against it
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Resident replaced customary district chiefs with salaried officers and taxed the river trade; from 1891 to 1895 much of the interior was in armed revolt against exactly those changes.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Pekan and Kuala Lipis, under the Governor at Singapore

statusPeriods.label: Federated Malay State
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Pahang was the poorest of the four federated states and was subsidised by Perak and Selangor tin money; its own economy was gold, tin at Sungai Lembing and, later, rubber.

statusPeriods.label: Japanese occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Japanese forces landed at Kuantan on 31 December 1941 and held Pahang for the rest of the war; the state's jungle later sheltered both anti-Japanese and, after 1948, anti-British guerrillas.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Enemy occupation; British authority was zero.

statusPeriods.label: Malayan Union, then Federation of Malaya
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Pahang passed through the Malayan Union and the 1948 Federation; its forests were a main theatre of the Emergency, and the British High Commissioner Henry Gurney was ambushed and killed on the road to Fraser's Hill in October 1951.
statusPeriods.franchise: Federal elections in 1955 on a citizenship register.

departures.how: Pahang became independent as a state of the Federation of Malaya, 69 years after a killing at Pekan was used to justify sending its first Resident.

geoCoverage.label: The southern tip of the peninsula

acquisitions.how: Sultan Abu Bakar signed a treaty in London that gave Britain control of Johor's foreign relations and promised British protection, on terms he negotiated himself and which kept British officials out of his government for another 29 years.

counterparties.name: The Sultanate of Johor
counterparties.lost: Its right to deal with any foreign power except through Britain. Abu Bakar had spent twenty years making Johor look like a modern state precisely so that London would treat him as a ruler rather than a chief, and it worked longer than anywhere else on the peninsula.
counterparties.note: The 1885 treaty was far lighter than the Pangkor terms: Johor accepted a consular agent, not a Resident with power over its revenue.

people.role: ruler who modernised Johor's administration and negotiated the lightest protectorate terms in Malaya

counterparties.name: The Sultanate of Johor
counterparties.lost: Internal self-government. From 1914 a British General Adviser sat in the state council and Johor's laws, budget and appointments needed his agreement.
counterparties.note: Johor was the last Malay state to accept a British adviser, 40 years after Perak.

statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. The 1895 constitution created a Council of State and a Council of Ministers appointed by the Sultan.
statusPeriods.note: Abu Bakar was received by Queen Victoria, travelled Europe, and used British society against British officials: Colonial Office files complain repeatedly that he went over their heads.

statusPeriods.label: Unfederated Malay State with a General Adviser

statusPeriods.governedFrom: Johor Bahru, under the High Commissioner at Singapore
statusPeriods.note: Johor's rubber estates and its causeway to Singapore, opened in 1923, made it one of the richest states in Malaya.

statusPeriods.note: UMNO was founded at Johor Bahru's Istana Besar on 11 May 1946 by Onn Jaafar, a Johor civil servant and son of a Johor chief minister.

departures.how: Johor became independent as a state of the Federation of Malaya, having been the last Malay state to lose its self-government and the birthplace of the party that ended British rule.

pedagogy.hook: Malaysia's smallest state exists because Siam carved it out of Kedah in 1843 to punish a rebellious sultan. Britain inherited the line and never redrew it.

misconception.belief: Colonial powers drew all the borders in Asia.
misconception.correction: Perlis was created by Siam, not by Britain, and the Kedah-Perlis line predates British rule by 66 years. Empires very often froze borders that other states had drawn, and the freezing mattered as much as the drawing.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Perlis is the small case that proves a general rule: much of what looks like a colonial map is older lines that the empire found convenient and made permanent.

territories.formalName: The Colony of Labuan

modernSuccessors.name: Malaysia (Federal Territory of Labuan)
modernSuccessors.note: Part of Sabah from 1963, and a federal territory of Malaysia since 1984.

geoCoverage.label: A 91-square-kilometre island off Brunei Bay

acquisitions.how: Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddin II of Brunei ceded Labuan to Queen Victoria after a British squadron had shelled his capital the year before, and James Brooke and Captain Rodney Mundy raised the flag on Christmas Eve 1846.

counterparties.name: The Sultanate of Brunei
counterparties.lost: The island that commanded the approach to its own capital, ceded in perpetuity under the guns of a navy that had bombarded Brunei Town in July 1846.
counterparties.note: The cession was part of a settlement in which Brunei also accepted British suppression of what Britain called piracy and Brunei regarded as its own maritime authority.

instrument.name: Treaty of Labuan
instrument.note: Signed 18 December 1846; possession taken and the flag raised on 24 December.

people.name: James Brooke
people.role: Rajah of Sarawak; pushed the cession and became Labuan's first Governor in 1848

people.name: Rodney Mundy
people.role: Royal Navy captain who took formal possession

people.name: Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddin II
people.role: ruler of Brunei who ceded the island after the bombardment of his capital

acquisitions.resistance: Brunei's court resisted for two years; the bombardment of Brunei Town in July 1846 and the killing of the anti-British minister Pengiran Yusuf ended the argument.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony for coal that never came
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Governor answering to the Colonial Office ruled an island Britain had taken to be a coaling station and a naval base; the coal seams were poor, the harbour never rivalled Singapore, and the colony cost more than it earned every year.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Victoria, Labuan, under the Colonial Office
statusPeriods.note: James Brooke held two jobs at once: Rajah of independent Sarawak and Her Majesty's Governor of Labuan. Nobody in London seems to have thought this odd.

statusPeriods.label: Administered by the British North Borneo Company
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Tired of paying for it, the Colonial Office handed Labuan to the chartered company that ran North Borneo; the company let the courts and the coal trade decay and gave it back after seventeen years.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Sandakan, under the British North Borneo Company

statusPeriods.label: A settlement of the Straits Settlements, 1,300 km away
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Labuan was attached to the crown colony of the Straits Settlements and governed from Singapore, a thousand miles away across the South China Sea, by a Resident with a tiny staff.

statusPeriods.label: Japanese occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Japanese forces landed on 3 January 1942 and renamed the island Maida; Australian troops retook it on 10 June 1945, and the Japanese surrender of Borneo was signed there on 10 September 1945.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Enemy occupation; British authority was zero.

statusPeriods.label: Part of the Colony of North Borneo
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: In 1946 Labuan was attached to the new crown colony of North Borneo and governed from Jesselton; it went into Malaysia with Sabah in 1963.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Jesselton (Kota Kinabalu), under the Colonial Office
statusPeriods.franchise: Local council elections from 1962; no direct territory-wide election before Malaysia.

departures.how: Labuan left British rule as part of North Borneo when Malaysia was formed on 16 September 1963, 117 years after a Sultan under naval bombardment signed it away.

led.name: Donald Stephens

consequences.economicLegacy: Labuan was taken for coal that turned out to be poor and a harbour that never beat Singapore; it lost money for the Crown, then for a company, then for the Crown again, and became profitable only as an offshore financial centre after 1990.

misconception.belief: Britain took territory because it expected to profit from it, and generally did.
misconception.correction: Labuan was meant to be the Singapore of Borneo. The coal was poor, the harbour was empty, and the colony ran at a loss for so long that the Colonial Office gave it to a company in 1890 and only took it back in 1907 when the company let it fall apart.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: One small island shows the whole administrative filing system of empire: crown colony, then chartered company, then a distant crown colony's outlying settlement, then part of a Borneo colony, then a state of Malaysia — five arrangements in 117 years, with nobody local ever asked.

territories.name: Sarawak
territories.formalName: The Raj of Sarawak, later the Colony of Sarawak

namesOverTime.name: Sarawak Proper
namesOverTime.note: At first only the Kuching river district; the Brooke state grew by nine further cessions from Brunei between 1853 and 1905.

namesOverTime.name: Sarawak
namesOverTime.note: A state of Malaysia, with its own immigration control and a claim to a special constitutional position under the Malaysia Agreement.

geoCoverage.label: The Brooke state, grown from one river to a country
geoCoverage.change: The drawn shape is the modern state. Brooke Sarawak began as the Kuching river district in 1841 and reached these boundaries only in 1905, after nine separate cessions from Brunei.

acquisitions.how: James Brooke, an English adventurer with an armed schooner, helped Brunei's governor put down a rebellion of Bidayuh and Malay chiefs and then demanded the province as payment, becoming Rajah of Sarawak at 38.

counterparties.name: The Sultanate of Brunei
counterparties.lost: The first slice of an empire that had once covered most of Borneo. Over the next 64 years the Brooke family took nine more slices, until Brunei was two patches of coast surrounded by Sarawak.
counterparties.note: Each cession was paid for with a small annual sum. Brunei's rulers signed because refusing meant war with a state backed, informally, by the Royal Navy.

counterparties.name: The Bidayuh, Iban and Malay communities of the Sarawak river
counterparties.lost: The rebellion they had raised against Brunei's tax collectors ended with a new ruler instead of none, and Brooke's punitive expeditions over the following decades burned longhouses along the Skrang, Saribas and Rejang rivers.
counterparties.note: Britain officially had nothing to do with this. Brooke was a private citizen and Sarawak was, in law, an independent state until 1946.

instrument.name: Grant of the government of Sarawak by Pengiran Muda Hashim to James Brooke
instrument.note: Confirmed by Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddin II in 1842. Accounts differ on whether the decisive act was in July, September or the 1842 confirmation.

people.name: James Brooke
people.role: first White Rajah, 1841-68; a former East India Company officer who bought a schooner and made himself a king

people.name: Pengiran Muda Hashim
people.role: Brunei governor who granted Sarawak to Brooke and was later killed in a court coup

people.name: Rentap
people.role: Iban leader who fought three British-led expeditions and held the hill fort of Sadok until 1861

people.name: Sharif Masahor
people.role: Malay chief of Sarikei who led the resistance of 1859-60 and was exiled to Singapore

acquisitions.resistance: Iban and Malay resistance ran for thirty years: Rentap's fort at Sadok fell only to a third expedition in 1861, and in February 1857 Chinese gold miners from Bau stormed Kuching and burned the fort, forcing Brooke to swim the river to escape.

contested.note: The date Brooke became Rajah is given as 18 September or 24 September 1841 in different accounts, with a further ceremony in 1842. The Brooke government itself later celebrated 24 September.

evidence.author: Steven Runciman
evidence.work: The White Rajahs: A History of Sarawak from 1841 to 1946
evidence.supports: How the Brookes took Sarawak, the expansion from Brunei and the dynasty's rule.

acquisitions.how: Britain made Sarawak a protectorate in 1888, taking over its foreign relations while leaving the Brooke family in complete control of everything inside it.

counterparties.name: The Raj of Sarawak under Charles Brooke
counterparties.lost: Its independence in foreign affairs. Britain acted partly to stop the Brookes and the British North Borneo Company carving up Brunei entirely, and partly to keep other European powers out of Borneo.
counterparties.note: The protectorate made Sarawak's peculiar status official: a British-protected state ruled by an English family who were not British officials and took no orders from London.

instrument.name: Agreement of Protection between Great Britain and Sarawak

acquisitions.how: The third Rajah, Vyner Brooke, sold his country to Britain for a pension after the war, and the Council Negri approved the cession by 19 votes to 16, with every Malay and most Iban members voting against.

counterparties.name: The people of Sarawak, through the Council Negri
counterparties.lost: The 1941 constitution, in which the Brookes had promised self-government, was set aside; a state that had never been a colony became one at the moment other colonies were preparing to leave.
counterparties.note: The vote passed only because the European official members of the Council voted for it. Three hundred and thirty-eight Malay civil servants resigned in protest.

people.name: Charles Vyner Brooke
people.role: third and last White Rajah, who ceded Sarawak to the Crown in 1946

people.name: Anthony Brooke
people.role: the Rajah's nephew and heir, who campaigned against the cession and was banned from Sarawak for fifteen years

people.name: Rosli Dhobi
people.role: seventeen-year-old member of the anti-cession youth group Rukun 13; stabbed Governor Duncan Stewart at Sibu on 3 December 1949

acquisitions.resistance: The anti-cession movement produced mass petitions, 338 resignations from the civil service and, on 3 December 1949, the fatal stabbing of Governor Duncan Stewart at Sibu; four young men were hanged for it in 1950.

contested.note: Whether the 1946 cession was legal is still argued in Sarawak. Critics say the Rajah had no right to sell a country the 1941 constitution had promised to its people, and that the Council Negri majority depended on British officials' votes.

statusPeriods.label: An independent state ruled by an Englishman
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Sarawak was not British. It was a sovereign state whose ruler happened to be a British subject, governed by his own laws and his own officers, with the Royal Navy occasionally helping out and the Foreign Office occasionally disowning him.
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. The Council Negri, founded in 1867, is one of the oldest legislative bodies in South-East Asia; its members were appointed by the Rajah.
statusPeriods.note: The United States recognised Sarawak as an independent state in 1850, Britain in 1864. James Brooke was simultaneously Rajah of Sarawak and Queen Victoria's Governor of Labuan.

statusPeriods.label: British-protected state under the Brooke Rajahs
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain handled Sarawak's foreign relations; the Rajah handled everything else, running a personal government of about a hundred European officers over half a million people through Malay and Iban headmen.
statusPeriods.note: The Brookes deliberately kept out plantations, missionaries in some districts and large-scale Chinese settlement, arguing they were protecting Sarawak's peoples. Sarawak stayed poorer and less developed than North Borneo as a result, and historians still argue about whether that was protection or paternalism.

statusPeriods.label: Japanese occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Japanese forces took Kuching on 24 December 1941; the Rajah was already abroad. Allied officers of Z Special Unit later organised Kelabit and Kayan resistance in the interior highlands.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Enemy occupation; neither British nor Brooke authority survived.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony of Sarawak
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British Military Administration ran the country until 15 April 1946; the Rajah then ceded it to the Crown, and a Governor with an appointed council governed against a sustained anti-cession movement.
statusPeriods.franchise: Sarawak's first elections were indirect: local councils elected in 1959 chose the members of the district and divisional councils that chose the Council Negri.
statusPeriods.note: For eighteen years Sarawak was the only new British colony taken on after 1945 anywhere in the world.

departures.how: Sarawak became independent by joining Malaysia, after a British-appointed commission and a United Nations mission tested opinion and found roughly a third strongly in favour, a third in favour with conditions and a third opposed or wanting independence first.

led.role: Iban leader of the Sarawak National Party and first Chief Minister of Sarawak

led.role: chaired the 1962 commission of enquiry into Borneo opinion

cost.note: Indonesia's Confrontation of 1963-66 was fought mainly along Sarawak's border: about 590 Indonesian, 114 Commonwealth and 36 civilian deaths are the usual published figures, and the Sarawak communist insurgency that grew out of the same conflict ran until 1990.

departures.borders: Sarawak entered Malaysia with the boundaries the Brookes had taken from Brunei, and with the 18-point safeguards on immigration, religion, language and land that Sarawak politicians still cite in every argument with Kuala Lumpur.

contested.note: Whether Sarawakians consented to Malaysia is disputed. There was no referendum: the Cobbold Commission took submissions in 1962 and a UN mission surveyed opinion in 1963. Supporters call that adequate; critics call it a consultation designed to produce a known answer.

violence.note: The Brooke state was built by punitive expeditions: longhouses burned along the Skrang and Saribas in the 1840s and 1850s, Rentap's fort stormed in 1861, and about a thousand Chinese killed in reprisals after the Bau miners' rising of 1857.

consequences.economicLegacy: The Brookes kept large plantations and outside capital out of Sarawak, so it entered the twentieth century with almost no export economy beyond oil at Miri, opened in 1910; the timber boom came only after 1963.
consequences.borderLegacy: Sarawak's border with Brunei, which cuts Brunei into two separate pieces around the Limbang valley the Brookes annexed in 1890, is one of the strangest lines in Asia and is still resented in Bandar Seri Begawan.

pedagogy.hook: For a hundred years Sarawak was ruled by an English family who called themselves Rajahs. The last one sold his kingdom to Britain in 1946, and a seventeen-year-old stabbed the new governor to death.

misconception.belief: Every territory on the imperial map was governed by Britain.
misconception.correction: Sarawak was not a British possession until 1946. From 1841 it was an independent state ruled by James Brooke and his heirs, recognised by the United States in 1850 and Britain in 1864, and after 1888 a British-protected state that still took no orders from London. Britain took it a year after the war it had fought partly for the principle of self-determination.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Sarawak is the clearest case anywhere of empire by private enterprise, and of the empire moving in the wrong direction: Britain's newest colony was created in 1946, a year before it left India, and the people who objected most loudly were hanged for it.

territories.name: North Borneo
territories.formalName: The State of North Borneo, later the Colony of North Borneo

namesOverTime.name: Sabah
namesOverTime.note: The name adopted at the formation of Malaysia; it appears in older Brunei usage for the northern coast.

modernSuccessors.name: Malaysia (state of Sabah)
modernSuccessors.note: The Philippines has maintained a claim to eastern Sabah since 1962 on the basis of the 1878 Sulu grant.

geoCoverage.label: The northern tip of Borneo
geoCoverage.change: Company authority reached the coasts and rivers long before the interior. The Murut and Dusun uplands were not effectively administered until after 1915.

acquisitions.how: An Austrian consul and a British merchant bought northern Borneo twice over — from the Sultan of Brunei in December 1877 and from the Sultan of Sulu in January 1878 — for annual payments of 15,000 and 5,000 dollars.

counterparties.name: The Sultanate of Sulu
counterparties.lost: Its claim to the north-east coast, for 5,000 dollars a year. The Malay word in the grant, padjak, can mean lease or cession, and that single word is the basis of the Philippines' claim to Sabah today and of a still-running arbitration by the Sultan's heirs.
counterparties.note: Malaysia paid the annual sum, by then 5,300 ringgit, to the Sultan's heirs until 2013.

counterparties.name: The Sultanate of Brunei
counterparties.lost: The last of its northern territories, for 15,000 dollars a year, leaving the sultanate reduced to a fraction of what it had held a century earlier.

counterparties.name: The Dusun, Murut, Bajau and Suluk peoples of North Borneo
counterparties.lost: Their land was sold by two sultans whose authority over the interior had always been nominal, to a company that then imposed a poll tax and land registration on people who had never paid either.
counterparties.note: It was the tax and the labour demands, not the sale, that produced Mat Salleh's rebellion in 1894 and the Murut rising of 1915.

instrument.name: Grant by Sultan Jamal ul-Azam of Sulu to Baron von Overbeck and Alfred Dent
instrument.note: The Brunei grant was signed on 29 December 1877. The Royal Charter incorporating the British North Borneo Company followed on 1 November 1881.

people.name: Alfred Dent
people.role: British merchant who bought out his partner and obtained the royal charter

people.name: Gustav von Overbeck
people.role: Austrian consul in Hong Kong who negotiated both grants

people.name: Sultan Jamal ul-Azam of Sulu
people.role: signed the 1878 grant whose wording is still disputed in international law

people.name: Mat Salleh
people.role: Bajau-Suluk leader who fought the company from 1894 and was killed at Tambunan on 31 January 1900

acquisitions.resistance: Mat Salleh burned the company's station on Gaya Island in 1897 and fought for six years before being killed at Tambunan; in 1915 the Murut leader Ontoros Antanum led a rising against forced labour and taxation that the company crushed with heavy loss of life.

contested.note: Whether the 1878 Sulu grant was a lease or a permanent cession is genuinely unsettled. The Malay text uses padjak; British, Malaysian, Philippine and Spanish translations differ, and the question has been argued in courts and arbitrations for over a century.

evidence.author: Ian Black
evidence.work: A Gambling Style of Government: The Establishment of the Chartered Company's Rule in Sabah, 1878-1915
evidence.supports: The grants, the charter and the company's imposition of taxation and its consequences.

statusPeriods.label: Chartered company government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A London company with a royal charter from 1881 raised its own armed constabulary, appointed its own governor, levied taxes and issued its own stamps and currency over territory it had bought from two sultans.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kudat, then Sandakan, under a board of directors in London

statusPeriods.label: British protectorate, still run by the company
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain took over foreign relations in 1888 and left the company to govern: for another 54 years, a private board in London appointed the men who taxed, judged and policed North Borneo.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: A protectorate in law, but the internal government was a chartered company rather than a local ruler, so the usual protectorate picture of a throne left standing does not apply here.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Sandakan, under the British North Borneo Company
statusPeriods.note: The company brought in Chinese, mostly Hakka, settlers for tobacco and rubber estates and Javanese and Timorese labour for the plantations; the shape of Sabah's population today was set by those recruitment drives.

statusPeriods.label: Japanese occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Japan took Sandakan on 19 January 1942 and ran North Borneo as part of its Borneo command; the Kinabalu guerrillas rose at Jesselton in October 1943 and were destroyed, with several hundred civilians executed in reprisal.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Enemy occupation; British and company authority were zero.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony of North Borneo
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The company, ruined and unable to pay for reconstruction, sold its rights to the Crown for about 1.4 million pounds; a Governor at Jesselton ran the colony with an appointed council from 15 July 1946.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Jesselton (Kota Kinabalu), under the Colonial Office
statusPeriods.franchise: Local authority elections were held in 1962; there was never a territory-wide election under British rule.
statusPeriods.note: Sandakan and Jesselton had been flattened by Allied bombing and the colony's first task was rebuilding towns its own side had destroyed.

departures.how: North Borneo joined Malaysia on 16 September 1963 with twenty conditions attached, after the Cobbold Commission and a United Nations mission reported majority support and the Philippines and Indonesia both objected.

departures.borders: Sabah entered Malaysia with the boundaries the chartered company had bought in 1877 and 1878 — and with a live Philippine claim to the east coast, based on whether one word in the Sulu grant meant lease or sale.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: One word in a document signed in 1878 — padjak, meaning lease or cession depending on who translates it — still shapes relations between Malaysia and the Philippines and produced an armed incursion in 2013. Colonial paperwork is not finished business.

keyDates.what: The Sultan of Sulu's grant, whose wording is still disputed
The British North Borneo Company gets its royal charter
Mat Salleh killed at Tambunan after six years of rebellion
The Sandakan death marches: of 2,434 prisoners, six survive
The bankrupt company sells out; North Borneo becomes a crown colony
Joins Malaysia as Sabah

territories.name: Brunei
territories.formalName: The State of Brunei Darussalam

modernSuccessors.name: Brunei Darussalam
modernSuccessors.note: An absolute monarchy under a sultanate that has ruled since the fifteenth century; the state of emergency declared in December 1962 has never been lifted.

geoCoverage.label: Two coastal enclaves, all that was left of an empire
geoCoverage.change: The drawn shape is what Brunei still held in 1888 after 47 years of cessions to the Brookes and the North Borneo Company: about 5,765 square kilometres, split in two by Sarawak's Limbang district.

acquisitions.how: Sultan Hashim Jalilul Alam accepted a British protectorate to stop Sarawak and the North Borneo Company swallowing what remained of his state; Britain took his foreign relations and did not stop the Brookes taking Limbang two years later.

counterparties.name: The Sultanate of Brunei
counterparties.lost: Control of its own foreign relations, and — despite the protection promised — the Limbang valley, annexed by Charles Brooke of Sarawak in 1890 without Brunei's consent and never recognised by it.
counterparties.note: Brunei had ruled most of Borneo and parts of the Philippines in the sixteenth century. By 1890 it was two pieces of coast, and the piece that divided them had been taken by the state it had itself created in 1841.

instrument.name: Protectorate Agreement between Great Britain and Brunei

people.name: Sultan Hashim Jalilul Alam Aqamaddin
people.role: sought British protection in 1888 and protested unavailingly at the annexation of Limbang in 1890

people.name: Charles Brooke
people.role: second Rajah of Sarawak, who annexed Limbang in 1890 and cut Brunei in two

acquisitions.resistance: Brunei protested to London for years over Limbang and refused to accept the annexation; the Sultan's petitions were forwarded, considered and denied.

acquisitions.how: Britain imposed a Resident on Brunei in 1906 whose advice had to be taken on everything except Malay religion and custom, the same formula used in Perak 32 years earlier, and so began governing the state directly.

counterparties.name: The Sultanate of Brunei
counterparties.lost: Internal self-government. The Sultan kept religion and custom; the Resident took revenue, appointments, land and law.
counterparties.note: Britain acted because the alternative was that Brunei would collapse and be partitioned between Sarawak and North Borneo, which the Colonial Office had begun to think would look bad.

instrument.name: Supplementary Protectorate Agreement of 1905-06
instrument.note: Signed 3 December 1905 and brought into effect on 2 January 1906 with the arrival of the first Resident.

statusPeriods.label: Protected state without a Resident
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain controlled Brunei's dealings with other states and otherwise left the Sultan alone — including, in practice, leaving him alone while Sarawak annexed his richest district.

statusPeriods.label: British Residency
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British Resident ran the government, reorganised the land and tax system and abolished the old system of tax-farming districts to nobles; oil was found at Seria in 1929 and transformed the state's finances.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Brunei Town, under the High Commissioner for the Malay States and then the Governor of the Straits Settlements

statusPeriods.label: Japanese occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Japanese forces landed at Kuala Belait on 16 December 1941 to take the oilfields; Australian troops of the 9th Division landed at Brunei Bay on 10 June 1945 to take them back.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Enemy occupation; British authority was zero.

statusPeriods.label: Residency restored
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British military administration to July 1946, then the Residency again, with the Seria oilfield rebuilt and Brunei rapidly becoming the richest place per head in South-East Asia.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Brunei Town, under the Governor of Sarawak as High Commissioner

statusPeriods.label: Internal self-government under the Sultan
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The 1959 constitution ended the Residency and gave the Sultan control of internal affairs, leaving Britain defence and foreign policy; after the revolt of December 1962 the Sultan ruled by emergency decree, and has ever since.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Brunei Town (Bandar Seri Begawan), with a British High Commissioner
statusPeriods.franchise: Indirect elections for a partly elected council were held in 1962. The Parti Rakyat Brunei won every elected seat, was never allowed to take office, and rose in revolt in December.
statusPeriods.note: British Gurkha troops flown from Singapore put down the 1962 revolt within about a week. The emergency proclaimed then has never been lifted, and Brunei has had no elections since.

departures.how: Brunei took full independence at midnight on 31 December 1983 under a treaty signed five years earlier, after refusing to join Malaysia in 1963 over oil revenues and the precedence of its Sultan.

led.name: Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah
led.role: Sultan from 1967; negotiated and proclaimed independence

led.name: Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddien III
led.role: Sultan 1950-67; kept Brunei out of Malaysia in 1963 and out of the 1962 rebels' hands

led.name: A. M. Azahari
led.role: leader of the Parti Rakyat Brunei, which won the 1962 election and then rose in revolt; died in exile in Indonesia in 2002

departures.movement: Negotiated between the Sultan and the British government; the mass party that had wanted independence sooner had been suppressed in 1962

cost.note: Independence in 1984 was peaceful. The revolt that shaped it was not: fighting in December 1962 killed dozens among the rebels and the British-led troops, thousands were detained, and some leaders were held without trial into the 1970s. Published casualty figures vary and no agreed total exists.

departures.borders: Brunei became independent as two enclaves separated by Sarawak's Limbang district, the shape Charles Brooke gave it in 1890 and which Brunei has never formally accepted.

instrument.name: Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation between the United Kingdom and Brunei
instrument.note: Signed in 1979 with a five-year run-up; independence took effect on 1 January 1984.

violence.note: The revolt of 8 December 1962, launched by the party that had just won every elected seat, was crushed by British and Gurkha troops flown from Singapore within about a week; thousands were detained and the emergency has never been lifted.

consequences.economicLegacy: Oil found at Seria in 1929 made Brunei rich enough to refuse Malaysia in 1963 and to run a welfare state without income tax; it also gave the Sultan the means to govern without a parliament.
consequences.borderLegacy: Britain's protectorate promised to defend Brunei and then allowed Sarawak to annex Limbang in 1890, splitting the country into two pieces — the most visible unresolved consequence of British rule in Borneo.

commonwealth.note: Brunei joined the Commonwealth on independence; its head of state is its own Sultan.

peak.populationNote: 1960 census of Brunei, rounded. The population was about 190,000 at independence in 1984.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Brunei’s largest recorded population: 84,000 people, counted in 1960.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Graham Saunders
evidence.work: A History of Brunei
evidence.supports: The sultanate's contraction, the protectorate, the Residency and independence.

evidence.author: D. S. Ranjit Singh
evidence.work: Brunei 1839-1983: The Problems of Political Survival
evidence.supports: How Brunei survived as a state between Sarawak and North Borneo, and the 1962 revolt.

pedagogy.hook: Brunei once ruled most of Borneo. By 1890 an English family's private kingdom next door had taken so much of it that the Sultan was left with two separate patches of coast.

misconception.belief: A protectorate meant Britain protected a state from being taken over.
misconception.correction: Brunei accepted British protection in 1888 precisely to stop Sarawak taking more of it. Two years later Sarawak annexed the Limbang valley anyway, cutting Brunei in half, and Britain declined to reverse it. Brunei has never accepted the annexation.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Brunei is the state that said no. It refused Malaysia in 1963, kept its oil, and became independent alone in 1984 — the last British-protected state in Asia, and the only one whose ruler ended up with more power than any colonial governor ever had.

keyDates.what: Brunei becomes a British protectorate
Sarawak annexes Limbang, splitting Brunei in two
Oil found at Seria
The Brunei revolt; British and Gurkha troops crush it in about a week
Brunei stays out of Malaysia
Full independence

territories.name: Siam (informal empire)
territories.formalName: The Kingdom of Siam under the unequal treaties

namesOverTime.name: Thailand
namesOverTime.note: Renamed Prathet Thai in 1939, briefly Siam again from 1946 to 1948, and Thailand ever since.

modernSuccessors.name: Kingdom of Thailand
modernSuccessors.note: The only country in South-East Asia never colonised by a European power.

geoCoverage.label: Never ruled, but not free either
geoCoverage.change: This is not British territory. It is drawn to show the empire's informal reach: a sovereign kingdom inside a treaty system Britain wrote, where British subjects were outside Siamese courts and Siamese tariffs were capped at three per cent.

acquisitions.how: Sir John Bowring, Governor of Hong Kong, arrived with a fleet behind him and got King Mongkut to sign a treaty capping Siamese import duties at three per cent, legalising the opium trade and putting British subjects outside Siamese law.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of Siam
counterparties.lost: Control of its own tariffs, its own courts over foreigners and much of its royal trading revenue. Siam kept its independence and paid for it with its fiscal sovereignty for the next eighty years.
counterparties.note: Every other Western power then demanded the same terms. By 1870 Siam had signed a dozen near-identical treaties.

instrument.name: Treaty of Friendship and Commerce between Great Britain and Siam (the Bowring Treaty)

people.name: John Bowring
people.role: Governor of Hong Kong; negotiated the treaty that opened Siam to British trade on British terms

people.name: King Mongkut (Rama IV)
people.role: signed the treaty, judging that conceding trade and law was cheaper than fighting a war he would lose

people.name: King Chulalongkorn (Rama V)
people.role: ceded territory to Britain and France in 1893, 1904 and 1909 and used the reprieve to build a centralised modern state

acquisitions.resistance: Siam's resistance was diplomatic and it worked: by playing Britain against France, hiring foreign advisers of many nationalities and reforming its own administration, the kingdom stayed sovereign while its neighbours did not.

evidence.author: Nicholas Tarling
evidence.work: Imperialism in Southeast Asia: A Fleeting, Passing Phase
evidence.supports: The unequal treaties, the buffer-state settlement and the 1909 territorial exchange.

statusPeriods.label: Sovereign state inside the British treaty system
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Nobody in London gave orders in Bangkok. British power worked through a capped tariff, consular courts, British advisers in the Siamese finance ministry, British capital in teak and tin, and the standing knowledge that the fleet was two weeks away.
statusPeriods.franchise: An absolute monarchy until the revolution of 24 June 1932; thereafter a constitutional monarchy dominated by the army.
statusPeriods.note: Siam gave up about half the territory it claimed to Britain and France between 1867 and 1909, including Laos and western Cambodia to France and the four northern Malay states to Britain. Independence was bought with land.

departures.how: Siam never became independent from Britain because Britain never ruled it: what ended was the treaty system, dismantled between 1909 and 1938 and finally closed by the Anglo-Siamese peace treaty signed at Singapore on 1 January 1946.

led.name: Pridi Banomyong
led.role: regent and leader of the Free Thai movement, whose wartime resistance let Thailand escape being treated as a defeated enemy

led.name: Prince Wan Waithayakon
led.role: Siamese diplomat who negotiated the 1946 settlement with Britain

led.name: Louis Mountbatten
led.role: Supreme Allied Commander South East Asia; Britain's post-war demands on Thailand were made through his command

cost.money: Britain demanded 1.5 million tons of free rice as reparations in 1945 and a veto on Thai rice exports; American pressure cut the demand down, and the final settlement was far smaller.
cost.note: No one was killed in the settlement. Thailand's war with Britain, declared on 25 January 1942, cost lives mainly among Allied prisoners and Asian labourers on the Burma-Siam railway inside Thai territory.

departures.borders: Thailand gave back the four Malay states Japan had handed it in 1943, and the Shan and Cambodian districts it had taken from Britain and France, returning to its 1941 borders.

instrument.name: Anglo-Siamese Peace Treaty, signed at Singapore

contested.note: This entry uses the vocabulary of 'departure' for something that was not one. Siam was never a British possession, so it never left; the atlas records the end of the unequal-treaty system instead. That the model has no better word for escaping informal empire is itself worth noticing.

consequences.borderLegacy: Almost every border Thailand has was fixed by treaties with Britain and France between 1893 and 1909. The southern one, drawn in 1909, left Malay-speaking Muslim provinces inside Thailand, where an insurgency has run intermittently since the 1960s.
consequences.economicLegacy: The three per cent tariff cap held for eighty years and kept Siam from protecting any industry; British firms took the teak forests of the north and much of the tin of the south, and Bangkok's rice exports were organised around British and Chinese shipping.

commonwealth.note: Thailand was never a British possession and has never been a Commonwealth member.

peak.populationNote: The 1911 Siamese census, the kingdom's first, gave about 8.3 million; coverage of the outer provinces was incomplete.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Siam (informal empire)’s largest recorded population: 8,300,000 people, counted in 1911.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Nicholas Tarling
evidence.work: Imperialism in Southeast Asia: A Fleeting, Passing Phase
evidence.supports: The treaty system, the buffer-state arrangement and the territorial settlements.

evidence.author: Chris Baker and Pasuk Phongpaichit
evidence.work: A History of Thailand
evidence.supports: The Bowring Treaty's effects, Chulalongkorn's reforms and the wartime settlement.

contested.note: Historians disagree about how far Siam was really independent. One view stresses that it kept its sovereignty and used the space to modernise; another argues that fiscal control, consular courts and foreign advisers made it a semi-colony in all but name. The map draws it as partial to keep the question open.

positions.claim: Siam preserved genuine independence by skilful diplomacy and internal reform, and the treaties were a price worth paying.
positions.heldBy: the traditional Thai national historiography and many Western diplomatic historians

positions.claim: Siam was a semi-colony: it lost tariff control, judicial authority over foreigners and half its claimed territory, which is what informal empire looks like.
positions.heldBy: historians of informal empire and Thai revisionists since the 1970s

pedagogy.hook: Thailand was never colonised — and it paid for that with half the territory it claimed, its tariffs, and the right to try foreigners in its own courts.

misconception.belief: A country was either colonised or it was free.
misconception.correction: Siam kept its king, its flag and its army, and still could not set its own import duties above three per cent, try a British subject in a Siamese court, or refuse a border demand backed by gunboats. Between 1867 and 1909 it gave up Laos, western Cambodia and four Malay states to stay sovereign. That is informal empire, and it covered far more of the world than the pink on the map.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Siam is the single best argument that the imperial map understates the empire. The pink shows where Britain ruled; it does not show where Britain set the tariff, judged its own citizens and drew the borders — which was most of the coast of Asia.

keyDates.what: The Bowring Treaty caps Siamese tariffs and exempts British subjects from Siamese courts
French gunboats at Paknam force Siam to give up Laos; Britain does not intervene
Britain and France agree to keep the Chao Phraya basin as a buffer between their empires
Siam trades Kedah, Perlis, Kelantan and Terengganu for legal concessions and a loan
The Anglo-Siamese peace treaty closes the treaty era

territories.name: Southern Indochina (British occupation, 1945)
territories.formalName: The British occupation of French Indochina south of the 16th parallel

modernSuccessors.name: Socialist Republic of Vietnam
modernSuccessors.note: France returned in 1945-46 and fought until 1954; the country was divided until 1975 and reunified in 1976.

geoCoverage.label: South of the 16th parallel only
geoCoverage.change: The Potsdam conference split Indochina at the 16th parallel: Chinese Nationalist forces took the Japanese surrender in the north, British and Indian forces in the south. The map has no unit for half a country, so the whole is drawn as partial.

acquisitions.how: The 20th Indian Division under Major-General Douglas Gracey flew into Saigon to accept the Japanese surrender, found a Viet Minh government running the city, declared martial law, disarmed it, and released and rearmed French troops the Japanese had interned.

counterparties.name: The Democratic Republic of Vietnam and the Viet Minh committee in Saigon
counterparties.lost: The government it had declared on 2 September 1945. Gracey banned its newspapers, imposed martial law, and handed the administration of Saigon back to the French on 23 September.
counterparties.note: Britain's orders were to disarm the Japanese and restore order, not to decide Indochina's future. In practice restoring order meant restoring France.

counterparties.name: The Empire of Japan
counterparties.lost: Its garrison in southern Indochina surrendered, and was then kept under arms by the British and used for guard duties and patrols against the Viet Minh.

people.name: Douglas Gracey
people.role: commander of the 20th Indian Division; declared martial law in Saigon and rearmed French forces

people.name: Tran Van Giau
people.role: chairman of the Viet Minh's Southern Provisional Executive Committee in Saigon

people.name: Ho Chi Minh
people.role: declared Vietnamese independence in Hanoi on 2 September 1945, in the zone the British did not occupy

people.name: Jean Cedile
people.role: French commissioner flown in to reclaim Cochinchina for France

acquisitions.resistance: Viet Minh and other Vietnamese forces fought British, Indian, French and Japanese troops around Saigon from late September 1945; the general strike of 17 September and the fighting at Tan Dinh and in the Cite Herault marked the start of thirty years of war.

evidence.author: Peter Dennis
evidence.work: Troubled Days of Peace: Mountbatten and South East Asia Command, 1945-46
evidence.supports: The British occupation of southern Indochina, Gracey's decisions and the handover to France.

statusPeriods.label: Allied military occupation under South East Asia Command
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British and Indian troops held Saigon and the roads out of it under martial law, using surrendered Japanese units as auxiliaries, while French forces built up to take over.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Full military authority in and around Saigon, and none in the countryside; the occupation never claimed sovereignty and was over in six months.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Saigon, under South East Asia Command at Kandy

departures.how: Britain handed southern Indochina to France and pulled its last troops out in March 1946, having restored French rule over a country that had declared its independence six months earlier.

led.name: Douglas Gracey
led.role: handed the territory to French command and withdrew

led.name: Philippe Leclerc
led.role: French general who took over the reconquest of Cochinchina

cost.note: About 40 British and Indian soldiers were killed in the six-month occupation, with roughly 130 wounded; Vietnamese and French civilian deaths in the Saigon fighting of September and October 1945 ran into the hundreds and were never properly counted. The American OSS officer Peter Dewey, killed on 26 September 1945, is generally counted as the first American to die in Vietnam.

departures.borders: The 16th parallel that Potsdam drew for the surrender was not the border that lasted, but it established the habit of dividing Vietnam by a line agreed elsewhere; the 17th parallel followed in 1954.

violence.note: British commanders released and rearmed French soldiers, kept surrendered Japanese troops under arms to fight the Viet Minh, and fought the first battles of a war that ran until 1975.

consequences.borderLegacy: Britain's brief occupation restored France in the south and made a negotiated Vietnamese independence far less likely; the First Indochina War began in earnest that December.

peak.populationNote: A rough contemporary estimate for the area south of the 16th parallel; no reliable count exists for 1945.

evidence.author: Peter Dennis
evidence.work: Troubled Days of Peace: Mountbatten and South East Asia Command, 1945-46
evidence.supports: The occupation, its orders and the handover to France.

evidence.author: Christopher Bayly and Tim Harper
evidence.work: Forgotten Wars: The End of Britain's Asian Empire
evidence.supports: British reoccupation across South-East Asia in 1945-46, including Saigon, and its consequences.

contested.note: Historians disagree about how much choice Gracey had. Some argue he exceeded his orders and personally set the First Indochina War in motion; others that London and Mountbatten had already decided France would return, and that he was executing policy, not making it.

pedagogy.hook: The first Western soldiers to fight the Viet Minh were British and Indian, in 1945 — and they kept surrendered Japanese troops under arms to help them do it.

misconception.belief: Britain's empire in Asia ended in 1945 when Japan surrendered.
misconception.correction: In September 1945 British and Indian troops occupied Saigon, declared martial law, disarmed the Vietnamese government that had just proclaimed independence, released and rearmed French prisoners, and handed the country back to France. British soldiers were still dying there in 1946.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows the empire acting as the restorer of other empires. Britain had no intention of ruling Vietnam and every intention of making sure a European power did — which is one reason decolonisation in Asia took another thirty years and cost millions of lives.

keyDates.what: Ho Chi Minh declares Vietnamese independence in Hanoi
The 20th Indian Division arrives in Saigon
Rearmed French troops seize Saigon's public buildings
The last British and Indian troops leave

territories.name: Hong Kong
territories.formalName: The Colony of Hong Kong, later the British Dependent Territory of Hong Kong

from.note: The Cantonese name of a harbour and its village, meaning 'fragrant harbour', probably from the incense trade; the anglicised spelling was fixed in the 1840s.

modernSuccessors.name: Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, People's Republic of China
modernSuccessors.note: Governed under the Basic Law and the 'one country, two systems' formula agreed in 1984 for fifty years, to 2047.

geoCoverage.label: The island alone
With Kowloon south of Boundary Street
geoCoverage.change: The Convention of Peking, signed after British and French troops burned the Summer Palace, added the Kowloon peninsula and Stonecutters Island in perpetuity.

geoCoverage.label: With the New Territories, on a 99-year lease
geoCoverage.change: A 99-year lease of the mainland behind Kowloon and 235 islands took the colony from 90 to about 1,090 square kilometres — nine tenths of it rented, not owned.

acquisitions.how: Royal Navy landing parties raised the flag at Possession Point during the first Opium War, on the strength of a draft convention that both London and Peking then repudiated, leaving Britain in occupation of an island with no legal title for two and a half years.

counterparties.name: The Qing Empire
counterparties.lost: A garrisoned island of about 7,000 people, seized in a war Britain fought because the Qing government had destroyed 20,283 chests of British-owned opium at Humen, near Canton, rather than let it be sold in China.
counterparties.note: The Daoguang Emperor stripped the negotiator Qishan of his rank and sentenced him to death, later commuted. Palmerston sacked Charles Elliot for accepting so little, calling Hong Kong a barren island with hardly a house upon it.

counterparties.name: The fishing and farming communities of Hong Kong Island
counterparties.lost: Their land and their villages: about 7,450 people lived on the island in 1841, mostly Tanka boat people and Hakka and Punti villagers, whose land rights the new colony recognised only in part.

instrument.name: Convention of Chuenpi
instrument.note: Repudiated by both governments. The occupation therefore rested on nothing but possession until the Treaty of Nanking was ratified in 1843.

people.name: Charles Elliot
people.role: British plenipotentiary who took the island and was dismissed for settling too cheaply

people.name: Gordon Bremer
people.role: commodore who raised the flag at Possession Point

people.name: Lin Zexu
people.role: Qing commissioner who destroyed the opium stocks at Canton in June 1839 and was exiled for the war that followed

people.name: Qishan
people.role: Qing negotiator who conceded the island and was sentenced to death for it

evidence.author: Julia Lovell
evidence.work: The Opium War: Drugs, Dreams and the Making of China
evidence.supports: The origins of the war, the Chuenpi convention and its repudiation.

acquisitions.how: The Treaty of Nanking, signed aboard HMS Cornwallis with a British fleet at the gates of the city, ceded Hong Kong Island to Britain in perpetuity, opened five ports and imposed an indemnity of 21 million silver dollars.

counterparties.name: The Qing Empire
counterparties.lost: Hong Kong Island outright, five treaty ports, control of its own tariffs and 21 million silver dollars — the first of the treaties Chinese historians call the unequal treaties and the beginning of what is taught in China as the century of humiliation.

instrument.name: Treaty of Nanking
instrument.note: Ratifications exchanged on 26 June 1843, when Hong Kong formally became a British colony.

people.name: Henry Pottinger
people.role: British plenipotentiary who negotiated the treaty and became Hong Kong's first Governor

people.name: Qiying
people.role: Qing imperial commissioner who signed the treaty

acquisitions.resistance: The Qing fought and lost: British steam warships destroyed the fleets and forts of the Pearl River, took Chusan, Amoy and Shanghai, and cut the Grand Canal before Peking gave way.

acquisitions.how: At the end of the second Opium War, days after British and French troops burned the Qing emperor's Summer Palace, the Convention of Peking ceded the Kowloon peninsula south of what became Boundary Street, plus Stonecutters Island, in perpetuity.

counterparties.name: The Qing Empire
counterparties.lost: The peninsula facing the harbour, legalised opium imports, the opening of Tientsin, and the Summer Palace, looted and burned on Lord Elgin's orders on 18 and 19 October 1860.
counterparties.note: The same convention also legalised the emigration of Chinese labourers on British ships, opening the way for the indenture traffic to the Caribbean, Peru and South Africa.

people.name: James Bruce, Lord Elgin
people.role: British high commissioner; ordered the burning of the Summer Palace and signed the convention

people.name: Prince Gong
people.role: the emperor's brother, left in Peking to sign the terms

acquisitions.how: In the scramble for Chinese ports that followed Japan's victory of 1895, Britain leased 950 square kilometres behind Kowloon and 235 islands for 99 years, rent-free, on the argument that Hong Kong could not be defended without them.

counterparties.name: The Qing Empire
counterparties.lost: Administration of nine tenths of what became Hong Kong for 99 years, while keeping legal sovereignty over it — a distinction that decided the colony's fate a century later.

counterparties.name: The Punti and Hakka villagers of the New Territories
counterparties.lost: Their land was leased over their heads by a government in Peking; when British officials arrived to plant the flag in April 1899 the clans of Kam Tin, Ping Shan and Sheung Shui fought them for six days.
counterparties.note: About 500 villagers were killed and no British soldiers died. The iron gates of Kam Tin were carried off to Ireland as a trophy and returned in 1925.

instrument.name: Convention for the Extension of Hong Kong Territory (the Second Convention of Peking)
instrument.note: Signed 9 June 1898; the lease ran from 1 July 1898 for 99 years, expiring on 30 June 1997.

people.name: Claude MacDonald
people.role: British minister at Peking who negotiated the lease and chose the 99-year term

people.name: Tang Tsing-shi
people.role: leader among the Kam Tin clans who organised the armed resistance of April 1899

acquisitions.resistance: The Six-Day War of 14 to 19 April 1899: several thousand villagers with matchlocks and cannon fought British troops at Tai Po and Sheung Tsuen. About 500 were killed. Britain then guaranteed customary land tenure and clan law in the New Territories, which survive today.

evidence.author: Steve Tsang
evidence.work: A Modern History of Hong Kong
evidence.supports: The 1898 lease, the New Territories resistance and the settlement that followed.

statusPeriods.label: Military occupation with no legal title
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Naval and army officers governed an island Britain held by force alone; both governments had repudiated the agreement that produced the landing, and land was already being sold at auction before anyone knew whether Britain would keep it.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: the harbour, under the plenipotentiary and the naval commander

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony under a Governor
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Governor appointed in London ruled with an Executive and a Legislative Council he appointed; no Chinese resident sat on the Legislative Council until Ng Choy in 1880, and until 1904 Chinese people were barred by law from living on the Peak.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Victoria, Hong Kong, under the Colonial Office
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted for the Legislative Council in the whole of the colony's history. Hong Kong's people were never given a territory-wide vote under British rule.
statusPeriods.note: The colony grew on the China trade, on opium — the Hong Kong government ran an opium monopoly until 1943 — and on being the port through which Chinese emigrants left for the whole world. Its population reached 1.6 million by 1941.

statusPeriods.label: Japanese occupation
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Hong Kong surrendered on Christmas Day 1941 after eighteen days of fighting and was governed by a Japanese military administration; the population was deliberately driven out to reduce the number of mouths, falling from about 1.6 million to roughly 600,000 by 1945.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: Occupied by Japan: British authority was zero for three years and eight months. The data model's rule for enemy occupation applies.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony, then British Dependent Territory
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Governor with an appointed council governed a refugee city that became a manufacturing centre and then a financial one; London shelved the 1946 plan for an elected council, and direct elections to the Legislative Council came only in 1991, six years before the handover.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Victoria, Hong Kong, under the Foreign and Commonwealth Office from 1968
statusPeriods.franchise: No elections at all until 1985, when some seats were filled indirectly; the first directly elected seats came in 1991 and the last colonial election, under Chris Patten's widened franchise in 1995, was undone by Beijing in 1997.
statusPeriods.note: About a million refugees arrived from China after 1949. The Kowloon riots of 1956 and the leftist riots of 1967, in which 51 people died, shaped the reforming, interventionist government of the 1970s under Murray MacLehose.

departures.how: Britain handed the whole of Hong Kong to China at midnight on 30 June 1997, although only the New Territories were leased: without their land, water and food the ceded island and Kowloon could not function, and Deng Xiaoping had made clear he would take all of it in 1997 whatever the treaties said.

becomes.name: Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China

led.name: Margaret Thatcher
led.role: Prime Minister who opened the negotiations in Peking in September 1982 and conceded sovereignty in 1984

led.name: Deng Xiaoping
led.role: Chinese leader who insisted on full sovereignty and offered the 'one country, two systems' formula

led.name: Chris Patten
led.role: last Governor; widened the electoral franchise in 1994-95 against Chinese objections and saw it dismantled at the handover

led.name: Martin Lee
led.role: founder of Hong Kong's Democratic Party; argued Hong Kong people should have had a say in their own future and were never given one

led.name: Szeto Wah
led.role: teacher and legislator who led the movement for democracy and the annual Tiananmen vigil

departures.movement: Negotiated between London and Peking. Hong Kong's own people were not represented at the table and were never given a vote on the outcome.

cost.money: Britain conceded sovereignty over the ceded territories it had held since 1842 and 1860 without compensation, in exchange for the fifty-year guarantee written into the Joint Declaration.
cost.note: Nobody died at the handover. The events that shaped it killed people elsewhere: the 1967 riots in Hong Kong left 51 dead, and the killings in Peking on 4 June 1989 sent a million Hong Kong people into the streets and set off a wave of emigration.

departures.borders: The lesson is in the arithmetic: only about 92 per cent of the territory was leased, and the 8 per cent Britain owned outright could not survive without it. A colony taken in three pieces was returned as one.

instrument.name: Sino-British Joint Declaration on the Question of Hong Kong
instrument.note: Registered as a treaty at the United Nations on 12 June 1985. It guarantees Hong Kong's system for fifty years, to 2047. In 2017 China's foreign ministry called it a historical document with no practical significance; Britain rejects that reading.

contested.note: Whether Britain could have kept the ceded areas is argued about. Legally the 1842 and 1860 cessions were permanent; practically the ceded areas had no water supply, no food and no defensible border, China regarded all three treaties as void, and Deng told Thatcher he could take Hong Kong in a day. Historians differ on how hard Britain tried.

evidence.author: Steve Tsang
evidence.work: A Modern History of Hong Kong
evidence.supports: The 1982-84 negotiations, the Joint Declaration and the last colonial decade.

populationTransfer.note: Hong Kong was built by movement: Chinese emigration to the whole world passed through it after 1860, and roughly a million refugees arrived from China between 1945 and 1951, housed in squatter settlements until the Shek Kip Mei fire of 1953 forced the government into mass public housing.

violence.note: The colony's violent moments were the New Territories war of 1899, the strike-boycott of 1925-26 that shut the port for sixteen months, the Japanese occupation, and the leftist riots of 1967 in which 51 people died, including police officers and children killed by home-made bombs.

consequences.economicLegacy: A colony founded to sell opium into China ended as one of the world's largest financial centres; the government's opium monopoly funded it into the 1940s, and its low taxes and common-law courts are still its selling point.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English common law, an independent judiciary, and a civil service culture that the Basic Law promised to preserve to 2047 — the most consequential legal inheritance any British territory left behind.

commonwealth.note: Hong Kong was a colony, not a state, and joined nothing on leaving. It is the only major British territory transferred to another power rather than made independent.

peak.populationNote: The 1996 by-census gave about 6.4 million. The figure is rounded because the by-census count and the mid-year estimate differ.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Hong Kong’s largest recorded population: 6,400,000 people, counted in 1996.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Steve Tsang
evidence.work: A Modern History of Hong Kong
evidence.supports: The whole span from 1841 to 1997, the constitutional structure and the handover negotiations.

evidence.author: John M. Carroll
evidence.work: A Concise History of Hong Kong
evidence.supports: Colonial society, the Chinese business elite and the politics of the colony.

evidence.author: Julia Lovell
evidence.work: The Opium War: Drugs, Dreams and the Making of China
evidence.supports: The war that produced the colony and how it is remembered in China.

pedagogy.hook: Britain went to war to keep selling opium in China, and the prize was an island its own Foreign Secretary dismissed as "a barren island with hardly a house upon it".

misconception.belief: Britain gave Hong Kong back in 1997 because the 99-year lease on it ran out.
misconception.correction: Only the New Territories were leased, about 92 per cent of the land. Hong Kong Island and Kowloon had been ceded in perpetuity in 1842 and 1860 and were Britain's to keep. They were handed over anyway, because a city of six million cannot live on 8 per cent of its territory without water, food or a defensible border, and because China had never accepted that any of the three treaties were valid.
