pedagogy.whyItMatters: Hong Kong is the empire's clearest ending: not a nation becoming independent, but eight million people transferred from one sovereign to another without ever being asked. It is also the sharpest example of the empire's origins in the drug trade, and of what a colonial legal system can outlast.

keyDates.what: British forces occupy Hong Kong Island during the first Opium War
The Treaty of Nanking cedes the island in perpetuity
The Convention of Peking adds Kowloon, days after the Summer Palace burns
The New Territories leased for 99 years; villagers fight for six days in 1899
The Sino-British Joint Declaration promises fifty unchanged years
Hong Kong transferred to China

territories.name: Weihaiwei
territories.formalName: The Territory of Weihaiwei

modernSuccessors.name: People's Republic of China (Weihai, Shandong)
modernSuccessors.note: Returned to the Republic of China in 1930; Britain kept Liugong Island on a further lease for the navy until 1940.

geoCoverage.label: A naval harbour, an island and about 300 villages
geoCoverage.change: The drawn shape is approximate. The geometry could not reproduce the leased boundary, which ran ten miles inland from the bay and included Liugong Island; the published area was about 1,500 square kilometres.

acquisitions.how: Britain leased Weihaiwei from the Qing government to balance Russia at Port Arthur and Germany at Kiaochow, taking it the moment the Japanese army that had occupied it since 1895 marched out.

counterparties.name: The Qing Empire
counterparties.lost: A naval harbour on its northern coast and about 150,000 subjects, leased for as long as Russia held Port Arthur — a lease with no fixed end date, granted at the height of the scramble for concessions in China.
counterparties.note: In one year, 1897-98, Germany took Kiaochow, Russia took Port Arthur, France took Kwangchowwan and Britain took Weihaiwei and the New Territories. The Boxer rising followed in 1899-1901.

counterparties.name: The villagers of the Weihaiwei district
counterparties.lost: Their district was leased over their heads. When British officers surveyed the boundary in 1900 villagers attacked the survey party, and British troops killed a number of them before the line was fixed.
counterparties.note: Contemporary British reports give around twenty dead; Chinese accounts give more. No agreed figure exists.

instrument.name: Convention for the Lease of Weihaiwei
instrument.note: The lease was to run 'for so long a period as Port Arthur shall remain in the occupation of Russia' — meaning Britain in principle had to give it back after Japan took Port Arthur in 1905. Britain stayed another 25 years.

people.name: Claude MacDonald
people.role: British minister at Peking who negotiated both the Weihaiwei lease and the New Territories lease in the same summer

people.name: Reginald Johnston
people.role: district officer and then Commissioner at Weihaiwei; later tutor to the last Qing emperor, Puyi

acquisitions.resistance: Villagers fought the boundary survey in 1900, and the territory's Chinese Regiment, raised by Britain from local men, was used against the Boxers at Tientsin the same year — Chinese soldiers in British uniform fighting Chinese insurgents in a British-leased corner of China.

evidence.author: Pamela Atwell
evidence.work: British Mandarins and Chinese Reformers: The British Administration of Weihaiwei (1898-1930) and the Territory's Return to Chinese Rule
evidence.supports: The lease, the administration of the villages and the 1930 rendition.

statusPeriods.label: Leased territory under a Commissioner
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Commissioner and a handful of district officers governed about 150,000 villagers with almost no police, by hearing disputes through the existing village headmen and Chinese customary law; the Royal Navy used the harbour as its summer station.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Port Edward, Weihaiwei, under the Colonial Office from 1901
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. The villages kept their own headmen and their own courts of first instance, which is why the territory needed so few officials.
statusPeriods.note: Weihaiwei never became the naval base it was taken for; the fleet preferred Hong Kong and Singapore. Its main British legacy is a book: Reginald Johnston's Lion and Dragon in Northern China, written while he was administering its villages.

departures.how: Britain gave Weihaiwei back to the Chinese Republic on 1 October 1930 after eight years of negotiation, keeping only Liugong Island on a further ten-year naval lease.

led.name: Reginald Johnston
led.role: the last British Commissioner; handed the territory over and left China for good

led.name: Wang Zhengting
led.role: Chinese foreign minister of the Nationalist government who pressed the negotiations to a conclusion

led.name: Xu Zujian
led.role: the Chinese commissioner who took over the administration in 1930

departures.movement: The Chinese Nationalist campaign to abolish the unequal treaties, which also recovered the British concessions at Hankow and Kiukiang in 1927

cost.note: Nobody was killed in the rendition. It was a negotiated transfer, and Britain's own officials had argued for years that a territory with no naval use and no revenue was not worth the diplomatic cost of keeping.

departures.borders: The lease boundary vanished from the map. Weihaiwei is the one place where Britain's Chinese concessions were undone by negotiation rather than by war or revolution.

instrument.name: Convention for the Rendition of Weihaiwei
instrument.note: Signed 18 April 1930; the handover took effect on 1 October 1930.

retainedTerritory.note: Britain kept Liugong Island in Weihaiwei harbour on a renewable ten-year lease after 1930 so the navy could go on using the anchorage; the arrangement lapsed in 1940 when the fleet had other problems.

consequences.borderLegacy: Weihaiwei was one of four leased territories carved out of China in a single year. Three of the four went back within a generation; the fourth, the New Territories, decided the fate of Hong Kong.
consequences.economicLegacy: Britain built a summer resort, a courthouse and a hospital and almost nothing else; the territory ran a small deficit for most of its 32 years and was never developed as a port.

peak.populationNote: A round figure. British administrative returns give roughly 150,000 people in about 300 villages; no census on modern lines was ever taken.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Weihaiwei’s largest recorded population: 150,000 people, counted in 1911.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Pamela Atwell
evidence.work: British Mandarins and Chinese Reformers: The British Administration of Weihaiwei (1898-1930) and the Territory's Return to Chinese Rule
evidence.supports: The administration of the leased territory and its return.

evidence.author: Reginald Fleming Johnston
evidence.work: Lion and Dragon in Northern China
evidence.supports: How British officials actually governed the villages of Weihaiwei, written by one of them.

evidence.author: Robert Bickers
evidence.work: The Scramble for China: Foreign Devils in the Qing Empire, 1832-1914
evidence.supports: The 1897-98 scramble for leases and concessions in China.

contested.note: The territory's size is given differently in different sources — about 740 square kilometres for the mainland strip, roughly 1,500 including the islands and the ten-mile zone. The geometry available to this atlas is an approximation of the leased boundary, and the map should be read as indicative.

pedagogy.hook: The British official who spent thirteen years judging village disputes in Weihaiwei went on to become the last Emperor of China's private tutor.

misconception.belief: Britain's empire in China was Hong Kong.
misconception.correction: In 1898 alone Britain took two leases in China: the New Territories, which made Hong Kong viable, and Weihaiwei, 1,600 kilometres north in Shandong, held for 32 years and handed back in 1930. Britain also ran concessions in Shanghai, Tientsin, Hankow and half a dozen other cities. The pink on the map is only the part Britain owned.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Weihaiwei is the counter-example to Hong Kong: taken in the same year, by the same minister, on the same kind of lease — and given back by agreement in 1930, when Britain decided it was not worth the argument. It shows that imperial retreat could be quiet, early and voluntary when nothing valuable was at stake.

keyDates.what: Britain leases Weihaiwei as Japanese troops withdraw
The 1st Chinese Regiment is raised from local men; it fights the Boxers in 1900
Japan takes Port Arthur from Russia, the stated condition for the lease; Britain stays anyway
Weihaiwei returned to China by agreement

events.title: The Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824
events.summary: Britain and the Netherlands settled their quarrel over the Malay world by swapping colonies: the Dutch gave up Malacca and all claims north of the Singapore Strait, Britain gave up Bencoolen and all claims on Sumatra.
events.significance: It drew the line that is now the Malaysia-Indonesia border, split the Johor-Riau sultanate between two European empires, and made the Straits Settlements possible. Two countries that speak one language exist because of a bargain struck in London by men who had never been there.

places.name: London
places.note: Where the treaty was signed.

places.name: Malacca
places.note: Handed to Britain.

places.name: Bencoolen (Bengkulu)
places.note: Handed to the Netherlands.

people.name: George Canning
people.role: British Foreign Secretary who authorised the exchange

people.name: Stamford Raffles
people.role: founded Singapore in 1819 and so forced the negotiation

people.name: Sultan Abdul Rahman of Johor-Riau
people.role: ruler whose kingdom was divided by the treaty without being consulted

pedagogy.hook: Two European foreign ministers divided the Malay world with a line through a strait, and never asked a single Malay ruler what he thought.

misconception.belief: Borders in Asia were drawn along natural or ethnic lines.
misconception.correction: The 1824 line ran through the middle of one kingdom, the Johor-Riau sultanate, whose people spoke the same language and shared the same rulers on either side of it. It survives as the Malaysia-Indonesia border, and it explains why Malay is the national language of two countries.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the cleanest example in the region of empire as accountancy: territory traded like counters, with the consequences left on the map for two centuries.

evidence.author: Nicholas Tarling
evidence.work: Anglo-Dutch Rivalry in the Malay World, 1780-1824
evidence.supports: The negotiation and terms of the treaty.

events.title: The Pangkor Engagement
events.summary: Aboard a ship off Pangkor island, the Governor of the Straits Settlements recognised one claimant as Sultan of Perak on condition that he accept a British Resident whose advice must be asked and acted on in everything except Malay religion and custom.
events.significance: It invented the residential system that brought every Malay state under British control over the next 35 years, and its exception for religion and custom is the ancestor of the division of powers in Malaysia's constitution today.

places.name: Pulau Pangkor
places.note: The engagement was signed offshore, aboard HMS Pluto.

people.name: Andrew Clarke
people.role: Governor of the Straits Settlements; acted beyond his instructions from London

people.name: Raja Abdullah
people.role: recognised as Sultan of Perak in exchange for accepting a Resident

people.name: Raja Ismail
people.role: rival claimant, backed by many Perak chiefs, who was not at Pangkor

pedagogy.hook: Britain took Perak by choosing its king. The price of the throne was a British official whose advice could not be refused.

misconception.belief: Britain conquered Malaya.
misconception.correction: Almost none of the peninsula was taken by open conquest. It was taken by treaty, usually by intervening in a succession dispute or a mining war and installing the side that would sign. The fighting came afterwards, when the treaties were enforced.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Indirect rule was cheaper than conquest and easier to defend in Parliament. Pangkor is where Britain worked out the formula, and it was copied across the peninsula and beyond.

evidence.author: Emily Sadka
evidence.work: The Protected Malay States, 1874-1895
evidence.supports: The engagement, its terms and its use as a template.

events.title: The killing of Birch and the Perak War
events.summary: Perak chiefs killed the first British Resident, J. W. W. Birch, at Pasir Salak on 2 November 1875. Britain brought troops from India, Hong Kong and the Straits, occupied the state, hanged three of the leaders and exiled the Sultan to the Seychelles.
events.significance: It settled whether a Malay state could refuse the residential system by force. It could not — and after 1876 no ruler on the peninsula tried, which is why the rest of British Malaya looks so peaceful in the records.

places.name: Pasir Salak
places.note: Where Birch was killed while bathing in the river.

places.name: Matang, Taiping
places.note: Where Maharaja Lela and Dato Sagor were hanged in 1877.

people.name: James Wheeler Woodford Birch
people.role: first British Resident in Perak; killed at Pasir Salak

people.name: Dato Maharaja Lela
people.role: Perak chief who organised the killing; hanged in 1877 and a national hero in Malaysia today

people.name: Seputum
people.role: the man who speared Birch in his bathing enclosure

people.name: Dato Sagor
people.role: chief hanged with Maharaja Lela

people.name: Sultan Abdullah Muhammad Shah II
people.role: the Sultan Britain had installed; exiled to the Seychelles for complicity

toll.note: No proper count exists. British and Indian military losses were light; Perak losses in the punitive columns along the Perak river were not recorded. Three men were hanged in 1877 and several chiefs exiled.

pedagogy.hook: Eleven months after Britain imposed its first Resident on a Malay state, his own chiefs stabbed him to death in his bathhouse.

misconception.belief: Colonial officials were resented but obeyed.
misconception.correction: Birch was killed because he did what Residents were supposed to do: collect taxes directly, register land and abolish debt-bondage. That took the chiefs' income and their dependants at once. The men hanged for it have national monuments in Malaysia.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows what indirect rule cost the people whose power it replaced, and how quickly Britain escalated to troops when a treaty was resisted.

evidence.author: Emily Sadka
evidence.work: The Protected Malay States, 1874-1895
evidence.supports: The causes of the killing and the campaign that followed.

contested.note: Casualty figures for the Perak War are not recorded on the Malay side, and the extent of Sultan Abdullah's involvement in the plot was disputed at his trial and is disputed still.

events.title: The Pahang rising
events.summary: District chiefs displaced by Pahang's British Resident took to the forest under Dato Bahaman, Mat Kilau and Tok Gajah and fought a four-year guerrilla war along the Pahang and Semantan rivers before being driven into Siamese-held Kelantan and Terengganu.
events.significance: The longest armed resistance to British rule on the Malay peninsula. It forced Britain to garrison the interior, and it left Malaysia with three of its most enduring anti-colonial heroes.

places.name: Semantan, Temerloh
places.note: Dato Bahaman's district, where the rising began.

places.name: Kuala Lipis
places.note: The Resident's headquarters.

people.name: Dato Bahaman (Abdul Rahman)
people.role: chief of Semantan; led the rising and died in exile in Siam

people.name: Mat Kilau
people.role: war leader; reported killed in 1895, but a man claiming to be him came forward in 1969 and was officially accepted

people.name: Tok Gajah (Imam Perang Rasu)
people.role: senior chief and Mat Kilau's father

people.name: Hugh Clifford
people.role: British officer who pursued the rebels into Kelantan and Terengganu

toll.note: Deaths among the Pahang fighters and the British-led force were in the dozens rather than the hundreds, but no reliable count exists; British reports record their own casualties and estimate the rest.

pedagogy.hook: Mat Kilau was declared dead in 1895. In 1969 an old man in Pahang said he was Mat Kilau, and after an official inquiry the government agreed.

misconception.belief: Resistance to empire was led by rulers.
misconception.correction: Pahang's Sultan stayed in his palace. The war was fought by the district chiefs whose river tolls and followers the Resident had taken away, and by villagers who had to pay new taxes in cash instead of kind.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest evidence that indirect rule was not accepted quietly. It also shows who did the resisting: not the men at the top, who were bought, but the men one level down, who were not.

evidence.author: Barbara Watson Andaya and Leonard Y. Andaya
evidence.work: A History of Malaysia
evidence.supports: The causes, course and suppression of the rising.

contested.note: Whether the man recognised in 1970 was really Mat Kilau is not settled by evidence; the government inquiry accepted him, and Malaysian historians remain divided.

events.title: Mat Salleh's rebellion
events.summary: Mat Salleh, a Bajau-Suluk leader, fought the British North Borneo Company for six years over its poll tax, its trading licences and its claim to rule land bought from two distant sultans. He burned the company station on Gaya Island in 1897 and was killed at Tambunan in 1900.
events.significance: The longest resistance to chartered-company rule in Borneo, and the clearest case anywhere of people taking up arms because a private firm had bought their country and started taxing them.

places.name: Gaya Island
places.note: The company station Mat Salleh burned in July 1897.

places.name: Tambunan
places.note: Where he was killed on 31 January 1900.

people.name: Mat Salleh
people.role: led the rebellion from 1894 until his death at Tambunan

people.name: Ontoros Antanum
people.role: Murut leader of the Rundum rising of 1915 against the same company and the same taxes

toll.note: Company records count their own losses in dozens. Deaths among Mat Salleh's followers and in the villages burned in reprisal were not counted.

pedagogy.hook: A company in London bought northern Borneo from two sultans in 1878. Sixteen years later the people who actually lived there started shooting.

misconception.belief: Indigenous resistance was hopeless and brief.
misconception.correction: Mat Salleh fought the company for six years and forced it to negotiate twice; the company gave him Tambunan valley in a settlement and then broke it. The Murut of the interior rose again in 1915. Company rule in Sabah was contested for its whole first generation.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows what a chartered company's sovereignty meant on the ground: a poll tax on people who had never paid one, collected by an armed constabulary working for shareholders.

evidence.author: Ian Black
evidence.work: A Gambling Style of Government: The Establishment of the Chartered Company's Rule in Sabah, 1878-1915
evidence.supports: The rebellion, its causes and the company's response.

contested.note: Mat Salleh's aims are read differently: company officials called him a bandit, later Sabahan historians a national resistance leader, and some scholars a chief defending his own trading position. All three readings use the same documents.

events.title: The Anglo-Siamese Treaty of 1909
events.summary: Siam transferred its claims over Kedah, Perlis, Kelantan and Terengganu to Britain. In exchange Britain gave up its extraterritorial jurisdiction over Asian British subjects in Siam and lent four million pounds for the Siamese southern railway.
events.significance: Half a million people changed empires by a document signed in Bangkok. It completed British Malaya, fixed the Malaysia-Thailand border, and left Malay-speaking Muslim provinces on the Thai side, where a separatist conflict has run since the 1960s.

places.name: Bangkok
places.note: Where the treaty was signed.

places.name: Alor Setar
places.note: Kedah's capital; its State Council recorded a protest.

people.name: Ralph Paget
people.role: British minister at Bangkok who negotiated the transfer

people.name: Prince Devawongse Varopakarn
people.role: Siamese foreign minister who signed away the four states to keep Siam's own independence

people.name: Sultan Abdul Hamid Halim Shah
people.role: ruler of Kedah, who was not a party to the treaty that disposed of his state

pedagogy.hook: Four Malay states were traded for a railway loan and some legal privileges. No Malay ruler was in the room.

misconception.belief: Empires expanded by conquering people.
misconception.correction: Britain gained four states and about half a million subjects in 1909 without firing a shot, by agreement with a third country that claimed them. Siam sold them to protect its own sovereignty, and it worked: Siam is Thailand and was never colonised.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the sharpest illustration of what sovereignty meant in the age of empire — something two governments could exchange for something else entirely.

evidence.author: Nicholas Tarling
evidence.work: Imperialism in Southeast Asia: A Fleeting, Passing Phase
evidence.supports: The negotiation, terms and consequences of the 1909 treaty.

events.title: The Bowring Treaty
events.summary: Sir John Bowring, Governor of Hong Kong, arrived at Bangkok with a fleet behind him and obtained a treaty capping Siamese import duties at three per cent, legalising the opium trade and placing British subjects under British consular courts rather than Siamese law.
events.significance: It made Siam part of Britain's informal empire without a single soldier landing: no flag, no governor, no colony, and no control over its own tariffs or courts for the next eighty years. Every other Western power then demanded identical terms.

places.name: Bangkok
places.note: Where Bowring negotiated with King Mongkut.

people.name: John Bowring
people.role: Governor of Hong Kong and British plenipotentiary

people.name: King Mongkut (Rama IV)
people.role: signed, judging that concession was cheaper than a war he would lose

pedagogy.hook: Britain took control of Siam's customs, courts and opium trade without taking one acre of Siamese soil.

misconception.belief: You can see the British empire on a map.
misconception.correction: The map shows where Britain ruled. It does not show Siam, where Britain set the maximum tariff and tried its own citizens in its own courts; or Argentina; or the Chinese treaty ports. Informal empire covered far more of the world than the pink did, and left far fewer traces on the atlas.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It defines the category of informal empire, which a student needs in order to see how big the British system actually was.

evidence.author: Chris Baker and Pasuk Phongpaichit
evidence.work: A History of Thailand
evidence.supports: The treaty's terms and its effect on the Siamese economy and state.

events.title: The First Opium War
events.summary: After the Qing commissioner Lin Zexu destroyed 20,283 chests of British-owned opium at Humen, near Canton - about 1,200 tonnes - Britain sent a fleet. Steam warships broke the Qing coastal defences, took Chusan, Amoy and Shanghai and threatened Nanking; the treaty that ended it took Hong Kong Island.
events.significance: It opened China to foreign trade by force, produced the first of the unequal treaties, and founded Hong Kong. In China it is taught as the beginning of the century of humiliation, and it remains the reason Britain's presence in China is remembered as it is.

places.name: Canton (Guangzhou)
places.note: Where Lin Zexu destroyed the opium in June 1839.

places.name: Nanking (Nanjing)
places.note: Where the treaty was signed aboard HMS Cornwallis.

places.name: Chuenpi
places.note: Where the repudiated convention of January 1841 was agreed.

people.name: Lin Zexu
people.role: Qing commissioner who seized and destroyed the opium and was exiled for the war that followed

people.name: Charles Elliot
people.role: British superintendent of trade; guaranteed the merchants' opium at government expense and so made it a British loss

people.name: Lord Palmerston
people.role: Foreign Secretary who ordered the expedition and sacked Elliot for settling too cheaply

people.name: William Ewart Gladstone
people.role: MP who told the Commons in April 1840 he knew of no war more unjust in its origin

toll.note: Chinese military deaths are usually put between 18,000 and 20,000 and are not securely counted; British and Indian losses were about 500, most from disease. Civilian deaths were not counted. The imbalance is the point: this was an artillery war against forts built for a different century.

pedagogy.hook: Gladstone told the House of Commons in 1840 that he knew of no war more unjust in its origin. Parliament voted for it anyway, by nine votes.

misconception.belief: The Opium War was about free trade in general, not opium in particular.
misconception.correction: The immediate cause was the destruction of 20,283 chests of opium - about 1,200 tonnes - that British merchants were smuggling into China against Chinese law. Elliot had promised the merchants government compensation, which turned a private loss into a public grievance. The treaty did not legalise opium; the second war, in 1860, did that.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the origin of Hong Kong, of the treaty-port system and of modern Chinese nationalism's account of the West. Every argument about Hong Kong since 1997 reaches back to it.

evidence.author: Julia Lovell
evidence.work: The Opium War: Drugs, Dreams and the Making of China
evidence.supports: The war's causes, conduct and its place in Chinese national memory.

evidence.author: Robert Bickers
evidence.work: The Scramble for China: Foreign Devils in the Qing Empire, 1832-1914
evidence.supports: The Canton trade system and the war's consequences for foreign presence in China.

contested.note: Historians differ on weighting: some stress opium as the cause, others the wider British demand for diplomatic equality and open trade. Nobody disputes that the trigger was the destruction of the opium or that Britain fought to keep the traffic possible.

events.title: The Second Opium War and the burning of the Summer Palace
events.summary: Britain and France went to war with the Qing over the boarding of the Arrow and wider demands for access. In October 1860 their armies entered Peking and Lord Elgin ordered the Summer Palace looted and burned in reprisal for the killing of prisoners.
events.significance: The Convention of Peking that ended it added Kowloon to Hong Kong, legalised the opium trade, opened Tientsin and allowed the recruitment of Chinese labour on foreign ships — beginning the indenture traffic that carried Chinese workers to the Caribbean, Peru and South Africa.

places.name: Yuanmingyuan, the Summer Palace, Peking
places.note: Looted and burned on 18 and 19 October 1860.

places.name: Kowloon
places.note: Ceded in perpetuity by the resulting convention.

people.name: James Bruce, Lord Elgin
people.role: British high commissioner who ordered the burning of the Summer Palace

people.name: Prince Gong
people.role: the Xianfeng Emperor's brother, left behind to sign the terms after the court fled

people.name: Charles Gordon
people.role: British officer present at the burning, who wrote that it was wretchedly demoralising work

toll.note: Battlefield deaths were in the low thousands, overwhelmingly Chinese. The destruction of the Yuanmingyuan is counted in objects rather than lives: thousands of items looted from it are in European and North American museums today, and China has campaigned for their return since the 1990s.

pedagogy.hook: In October 1860 British and French troops spent two days burning a palace complex the size of a town, and carried its contents home to museums where much of it still sits.

misconception.belief: Looted imperial objects are an African and Indian story.
misconception.correction: The 1860 sack of the Yuanmingyuan put thousands of Chinese imperial objects into European collections, and China raises it in cultural diplomacy to this day. The Pekingese dog breed reached Britain the same way: five were taken from the palace and one was given to Queen Victoria.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The second war, not the first, legalised the opium trade and opened the interior of China. It also added the part of Hong Kong that made the harbour defensible.

evidence.author: Robert Bickers
evidence.work: The Scramble for China: Foreign Devils in the Qing Empire, 1832-1914
evidence.supports: The war, the Convention of Peking and the expansion of foreign privilege in China.

events.title: The Six-Day War in the New Territories
events.summary: When British officials arrived to take possession of the newly leased New Territories, the Punti and Hakka clans of Kam Tin, Ping Shan and Sheung Shui fought them for six days with matchlocks, jingals and old cannon. About 500 villagers were killed; no British soldier died.
events.significance: The only battle ever fought on Hong Kong soil against British rule. It ended with Britain guaranteeing the villages their customary land law and clan rights, which is why the New Territories still has small-house rights and village elections today.

places.name: Tai Po
places.note: Where the flag-raising was attacked.

places.name: Kam Tin
places.note: Walled village whose iron gates were taken to Ireland as a trophy and returned in 1925.

people.name: Tang Tsing-shi
people.role: leader among the Kam Tin clans who organised the resistance

people.name: Henry Blake
people.role: Governor of Hong Kong, who ordered the occupation and then the concessions that followed it

people.name: James Stewart Lockhart
people.role: Colonial Secretary who surveyed the New Territories and recommended keeping Chinese customary law

toll.note: The usual figure is about 500 villagers killed, from later research on clan and government records; British forces suffered no fatalities. The one-sidedness reflects modern rifles and artillery against matchlocks.

pedagogy.hook: Hong Kong's only war of resistance lasted six days in 1899. About 500 villagers died and not one British soldier.

misconception.belief: Hong Kong was taken peacefully, unlike other colonies.
misconception.correction: The island was taken in a war, Kowloon in another, and the New Territories against six days of armed resistance by the people who farmed them. Britain then bought peace by guaranteeing clan land rights — a concession still visible in New Territories property law.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the moment when the lease stopped being paperwork. It also shows that a colonial government could be forced to compromise by resistance it easily defeated militarily.

evidence.author: Steve Tsang
evidence.work: A Modern History of Hong Kong
evidence.supports: The 1899 resistance and the land settlement that followed.

contested.note: The 500 figure comes from later research into clan and government records rather than a contemporary count; colonial reports at the time gave far lower numbers.

events.title: The treaty ports and the Shanghai International Settlement
events.summary: From 1843 Britain ran a network of privileged enclaves in Chinese cities where British law, British courts and British-appointed police applied to foreigners. The largest, the Shanghai International Settlement, was governed by a council elected by its foreign ratepayers.
events.significance: This was empire without colonies: no British flag flew over China, yet British subjects there were outside Chinese law, Chinese customs revenue was collected by a British-led service, and a foreign council ran the biggest city in the country. Leaving it off the map makes the empire look far smaller than it was.

places.name: Shanghai International Settlement
places.note: Governed by a Municipal Council elected by foreign ratepayers, with its own police force and volunteer corps. No polygon exists for it in this atlas; it is drawn as a point.

places.name: British Concession, Tientsin
places.note: One of nine foreign concessions in one city.

places.name: British Concession, Hankow
places.note: Returned to China in 1927 after Nationalist crowds occupied it.

places.name: Amoy (Xiamen)
places.note: One of the five ports opened by the Treaty of Nanking in 1842.

people.name: Robert Hart
people.role: Ulsterman who ran the Chinese Maritime Customs Service for 45 years, collecting China's tariffs for the Chinese government with a largely foreign staff

people.name: Chiang Kai-shek
people.role: Nationalist leader whose government recovered concession after concession from 1927 onwards

pedagogy.hook: For a century the biggest city in China was run by a council elected by its foreign residents, with its own police, its own courts and its own flag.

misconception.belief: Britain's empire in China was Hong Kong.
misconception.correction: Britain held concessions in Shanghai, Tientsin, Hankow, Canton, Amoy and elsewhere, ran the Chinese Maritime Customs Service, kept gunboats on the Yangtze a thousand kilometres inland, and exempted its subjects from Chinese law. None of it is coloured pink on an imperial map, and all of it was empire.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Informal empire is the category students most need and least often meet. Once you have it, the map stops being a picture of British territory and becomes a picture of British power, which is much larger and much stranger.

evidence.author: Robert Bickers
evidence.work: Britain in China: Community, Culture and Colonialism 1900-1949
evidence.supports: The treaty-port system, the Shanghai Settlement and the British community in China.

evidence.author: Jurgen Osterhammel
evidence.work: Semi-Colonialism and Informal Empire in Twentieth-Century China
evidence.publisher: in Wolfgang J. Mommsen and Jurgen Osterhammel (eds), Imperialism and After, Allen and Unwin
evidence.supports: The concept of semi-colonialism and how the treaty-port system worked.

contested.note: Historians argue about whether 'informal empire' is the right description for China: some say foreign power there was real but shallow and depended on Chinese collaboration; others that semi-colonialism understates how much of the Chinese state's revenue and law was under foreign management.

events.title: The Tok Janggut rising
events.summary: Villagers around Pasir Puteh in Kelantan refused a new British-designed land tax and the district officer system that came with it. Led by Haji Mohd Hassan bin Munas, known as Tok Janggut, they killed a police officer and held the district for weeks before troops from Singapore broke them up.
events.significance: The sharpest armed resistance in the northern Malay states, six years after Siam had handed them to Britain without asking. Tok Janggut's body was taken to Kota Bharu and displayed, and he became a national hero in independent Malaysia.

places.name: Pasir Puteh
places.note: Where the rising began.

places.name: Kota Bharu
places.note: Where Tok Janggut's body was displayed.

people.name: Haji Mohd Hassan bin Munas (Tok Janggut)
people.role: led the rising and was killed on 25 May 1915

people.name: Engku Besar Jeram
people.role: local noble who joined the rising and was exiled to Siam

people.name: William Langham-Carter
people.role: British Adviser in Kelantan whose land rents and district system triggered the revolt

toll.note: A police sergeant was killed at the start and a small number of villagers in the fighting; British reports give single figures, Kelantanese accounts give more. No agreed total exists.

pedagogy.hook: Britain got Kelantan from Siam in 1909 without asking anyone who lived there. Six years later the peasants of Pasir Puteh answered.

misconception.belief: People rebel against foreign rule because it is foreign.
misconception.correction: The trigger in Kelantan was a land rent payable in cash and a permit system administered by salaried outsiders. Sovereignty had changed in 1909 with barely a ripple; it was the tax collector, six years later, who produced the rising.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows where empire touched people's lives — in the land office, not the palace — and it is the reason Kelantan remembers 1915 rather than 1909.

evidence.author: Cheah Boon Kheng
evidence.work: To' Janggut: Legends, Histories and Perceptions of the 1915 Rebellion in Kelantan
evidence.supports: The rising, its causes and the competing later accounts of it.

contested.note: Colonial officials called it a tax riot led by a local strongman; Malaysian national history calls it an anti-colonial rising. Cheah Boon Kheng's study shows how colonial officials and Malaysian national historians each rewrote the same events over the twentieth century.

events.title: The Terengganu peasant rising
events.summary: About a thousand Terengganu peasants marched on Kuala Berang behind a religious teacher, Haji Abdul Rahman Limbong, in protest at British land and forest rules that required permits and payment for clearing land their families had always used. Troops and police from Singapore dispersed them.
events.significance: The largest rural protest in the Malay states between the wars, and one of the clearest instances of empire experienced not as flags and governors but as land registration. Limbong was tried, then exiled to Mecca, where he died the next year.

places.name: Kuala Berang
places.note: The district office the marchers occupied.

places.name: Kuala Terengganu
places.note: The Sultan's capital, from which the British Adviser called for troops.

people.name: Haji Abdul Rahman Limbong
people.role: religious teacher who led the movement; exiled to Mecca, where he died in 1929

people.name: Sultan Sulaiman Badrul Alam Shah
people.role: ruler caught between his British Adviser and his own subjects

toll.note: Several marchers were shot dead when troops opened fire; contemporary reports give figures from a handful to about a dozen, and no reliable total exists.

pedagogy.hook: A thousand farmers marched on a district office because Britain had started charging them for permission to clear their own land.

misconception.belief: Colonial land policy was a technical matter of surveying and registration.
misconception.correction: Registration decided who owned what. In Terengganu, land customarily held by clearing and use became land held by permit and payment, and families who had farmed for generations discovered they were trespassers. That is what a thousand people marched about.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Land law is where empire was felt hardest and is studied least. Terengganu 1928 puts the mechanism in front of a student in a single afternoon.

evidence.author: Heather Sutherland
evidence.work: The Taming of the Trengganu Elite
evidence.publisher: in Ruth McVey (ed.), Southeast Asian Transitions, Yale University Press
evidence.supports: The administrative changes behind the rising and the state's reaction.

contested.note: Colonial reports treated the march as a religiously inspired disturbance; later Malaysian scholarship treats it as an organised anti-colonial peasant movement. The casualty figures were never established.

events.title: Japan's conquest of British Asia, 1941-42
events.summary: In under six months Japan took Malaya, Singapore, Hong Kong, British Borneo and Burma. British, Indian and Australian forces surrendered in numbers without precedent, and Asians across the region watched the empire that claimed to protect them collapse in weeks.
events.significance: The military defeat was recoverable; the loss of prestige was not. Britain returned in 1945 to societies that had seen white rule beaten by an Asian army, had been governed without it for three years, and had armed political movements of their own.

places.name: Kota Bharu
places.note: First Japanese landing, about 00:25 on 8 December 1941 — before the attack on Pearl Harbor.

places.name: Singapore
places.note: Surrendered 15 February 1942.

places.name: Hong Kong
places.note: Surrendered on Christmas Day 1941 after eighteen days.

people.name: Yamashita Tomoyuki
people.role: commanded the Japanese 25th Army in Malaya; took Singapore with a force smaller than the one that surrendered to him

people.name: Arthur Percival
people.role: British general who surrendered Singapore

people.name: Mark Young
people.role: Governor of Hong Kong, who surrendered on 25 December 1941 and spent the war as a prisoner

people.name: Mohan Singh
people.role: Indian Army officer captured in Malaya who founded the first Indian National Army from prisoners of war

toll.note: About 130,000 British, Indian, Australian and local troops became prisoners in the Malayan campaign alone, and about 1,500 Allied and 2,000 Japanese soldiers died in the eighteen-day battle for Hong Kong, with many more prisoners dying in captivity afterwards. Civilian deaths under occupation across the region — from massacre, forced labour and famine — ran far higher and were never counted.

pedagogy.hook: The Pacific war began on a beach in British Kelantan, more than an hour before the first bomb fell on Pearl Harbor.

misconception.belief: Singapore fell because its famous guns pointed the wrong way, out to sea.
misconception.correction: Most of the guns could turn, and some did fire inland; what they mostly had was armour-piercing ammunition meant for ships, useless against infantry. Singapore fell because Japan came down the peninsula by land and Britain had planned for an attack from the sea, and because the defenders had no air cover and no tanks.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: 1942 broke the assumption that British rule in Asia was permanent. Everything that follows — the Malayan Emergency, Indian independence, the Indonesian revolution — is shaped by the three years when it was gone.

evidence.author: Christopher Bayly and Tim Harper
evidence.work: Forgotten Armies: The Fall of British Asia, 1941-1945
evidence.supports: The campaign, the collapse of British authority and its effects on Asian opinion.

events.title: The fall of Singapore
events.summary: Japanese forces crossed the Johor Strait on 8 February 1942 and General Percival surrendered a week later at the Ford factory at Bukit Timah. About 80,000 British, Indian and Australian troops went into captivity in a single day.
events.significance: Churchill called it the worst disaster in British military history. The naval base built to make the empire in Asia defensible fell in seven days, and with it the argument that Britain could protect Malaya, Australia or anyone else east of Suez.

places.name: Ford Motor Factory, Bukit Timah
places.note: Where the surrender was signed on 15 February 1942.

places.name: Sarimbun Beach
places.note: Where the Japanese 5th and 18th Divisions landed.

people.name: Arthur Percival
people.role: General Officer Commanding Malaya; surrendered a garrison larger than the attacking force

people.name: Yamashita Tomoyuki
people.role: Japanese commander, who bluffed at the surrender talks because his troops were low on ammunition

people.name: Gordon Bennett
people.role: Australian commander who left his division and escaped to Australia, and was condemned for it

people.name: Adnan Saidi
people.role: lieutenant of the Malay Regiment who held Bukit Chandu against far larger forces and was killed on 14 February 1942

toll.note: Roughly 5,000 Allied troops were killed or wounded in the week's fighting on the island, Japanese losses on the island were about 1,700 killed and 3,400 wounded. About 80,000 troops became prisoners; a large proportion of them, especially Indian and Australian prisoners, died in captivity on the Burma-Siam railway and elsewhere.

pedagogy.hook: Britain surrendered 80,000 men in one day to an army that was running out of ammunition and had fewer soldiers than the garrison it captured.

misconception.belief: The defenders were hopelessly outnumbered.
misconception.correction: Yamashita attacked Singapore with roughly 30,000 men against a garrison of about 85,000. He was short of shells and expected to have to bluff. Percival, who did not know that, surrendered. Numbers were not the problem; air power, tanks, training and command were.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the single moment students should attach to the end of the British empire in Asia. Nothing after 1942 could restore the assumption that Britain was able to defend the region.

evidence.author: Christopher Bayly and Tim Harper
evidence.work: Forgotten Armies: The Fall of British Asia, 1941-1945
evidence.supports: The campaign, the surrender and its meaning for British authority in Asia.

events.title: The Sook Ching massacre
events.summary: Within three days of taking Singapore the Japanese military police ordered all Chinese men between 18 and 50 to report for screening. Those judged hostile — former volunteers, teachers, Kuomintang supporters, sometimes men with tattoos or spectacles — were taken to beaches and shot.
events.significance: It is the defining atrocity of the occupation in Singapore and Malaya, and one of the reasons the Malayan Communist Party's anti-Japanese guerrillas commanded so much support among Chinese Malayans, which in turn shaped the Emergency after 1948.

places.name: Changi Beach
places.note: One of the execution sites.

places.name: Punggol Point
places.note: Another execution site.

people.name: Kawamura Saburo
people.role: commander of the Singapore garrison; tried in 1947 and executed

people.name: Tsuji Masanobu
people.role: staff officer widely held responsible for the screening order; never tried

people.name: Lee Kuan Yew
people.role: then a young man who passed through a screening centre and survived; described it in his memoirs

toll.note: Japanese officers testified at the 1947 war crimes trial to about 5,000 deaths. Singapore Chinese community surveys after the war put the figure at 25,000 to 50,000, including the massacres in Malaya. No count was possible, and the range itself is the honest answer.

pedagogy.hook: In two weeks of February 1942, men in Singapore were sorted at checkpoints by their hands, their tattoos and their spectacles, and those who failed were driven to the beaches.

misconception.belief: Japanese occupation was resented mainly because it replaced a milder British rule.
misconception.correction: The occupation was violent on a different scale: mass screening and execution of Chinese civilians, forced labour on the Burma-Siam railway, and famine. But Asians in Malaya also remembered that the British had evacuated Europeans from Penang and left everyone else, and neither memory cancelled the other.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It explains where the armed anti-Japanese movement's support came from, and therefore who Britain was fighting when it returned and declared an Emergency in 1948.

evidence.author: Cheah Boon Kheng
evidence.work: Red Star Over Malaya: Resistance and Social Conflict During and After the Japanese Occupation, 1941-1946
evidence.supports: The screening operations, their scale and their political consequences.

contested.note: The death toll is one of the most disputed numbers in South-East Asian history. The gap between the Japanese trial testimony of about 5,000 and community estimates of up to 50,000 has never been closed, and both figures are still cited.

events.title: The Sandakan death marches
events.summary: Of 2,434 Australian and British prisoners held at Sandakan in North Borneo, the survivors were marched 260 kilometres inland to Ranau in 1945 as Allied forces closed in. Those who could not walk were shot. Six Australians who escaped were the only survivors.
events.significance: The worst atrocity suffered by Australian servicemen in the Second World War, and a reminder that the war in British Borneo was fought on ground almost no one in Britain could find on a map. Local Dusun and Murut people who fed and hid escapers were executed for it.

places.name: Sandakan
places.note: The prisoner-of-war camp and airfield the prisoners were made to build.

places.name: Ranau
places.note: The end of the marches.

people.name: Hoshijima Susumi
people.role: camp commandant at Sandakan; tried and executed in 1946

people.name: Owen Campbell
people.role: one of the six Australian survivors, who escaped and was sheltered by local villagers

people.name: Wong Mu Sing
people.role: one of the local people who risked execution to feed and hide escaped prisoners

toll.note: Of 2,434 prisoners — about 1,787 Australian and 641 British — six Australians survived, all of them escapers. The figure is one of the best documented of the Pacific war because Australian war crimes investigators reconstructed it name by name.

pedagogy.hook: Two thousand four hundred and thirty-four prisoners were held at Sandakan. Six came home.

misconception.belief: The war in the Pacific was fought between Japan, America and Australia.
misconception.correction: It was also fought across British Borneo, Malaya and Burma, by British, Indian, Australian and local forces, and it was endured by the people who lived there. Dusun and Murut villagers who fed escaping prisoners at Sandakan were tortured and executed for it.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the concrete human cost of the imperial collapse of 1942 in a territory a private company had governed until 1946, and it is why Sabah's war memory is Australian as much as British.

evidence.author: Lynette Ramsay Silver
evidence.work: Sandakan: A Conspiracy of Silence
evidence.supports: The camp, the marches and the reconstruction of the death toll.

events.title: The Malayan Union and the birth of UMNO
events.summary: Britain merged the Malay states and the settlements of Penang and Malacca into one colony, took the sultans' sovereignty on signatures collected in six weeks, and offered citizenship to everyone born in Malaya. Malay protest destroyed it in 22 months.
events.significance: The only time Britain proposed genuine equal citizenship across race in Malaya, and the only time a British constitutional scheme in Asia was reversed by peaceful mass protest. It created UMNO, the party that governed Malaysia for the next 61 years.

places.name: Istana Besar, Johor Bahru
places.note: Where UMNO was founded on 11 May 1946.

places.name: Kuala Lumpur
places.note: Seat of the Union's Governor, whose installation the sultans boycotted.

people.name: Harold MacMichael
people.role: envoy who obtained the nine rulers' signatures between October and December 1945

people.name: Onn Jaafar
people.role: Johor official who organised the protest and founded UMNO on 11 May 1946

people.name: Edward Gent
people.role: the Union's only Governor

people.name: Tan Cheng Lock
people.role: Chinese Malayan leader who supported the Union's citizenship terms and founded the MCA when they were withdrawn

pedagogy.hook: Britain took nine sultans' sovereignty in six weeks and lost it again in twenty-two months, to men in white headbands who never fired a shot.

misconception.belief: Colonial governments did what they liked and were only stopped by violence.
misconception.correction: The Malayan Union was reversed by petitions, mass meetings, a boycott of the Governor's installation by all nine rulers, and pressure from retired British officials in London. Britain backed down completely. Two years later, faced with an armed communist movement, it fought for twelve years.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows what kind of opposition the empire responded to, and it created the political shape of modern Malaysia: a Malay party at the centre, and citizenship rules that decided who counted.

evidence.author: Tim Harper
evidence.work: The End of Empire and the Making of Malaya
evidence.supports: The MacMichael mission, the protest campaign and the replacement Federation.

events.title: The Malayan Emergency
events.summary: After three European planters were shot at Sungai Siput, Britain declared an Emergency and fought the Malayan Communist Party for twelve years. It moved about half a million rural Chinese into fenced New Villages, deported some 30,000 people to China, and hanged men for carrying arms.
events.significance: The war Britain won and left anyway. It became the model counter-insurgency campaign taught to armies for decades, and the reason 'Emergency' rather than 'war' was used: Lloyd's of London would not have paid out on plantation losses in a war.

places.name: Sungai Siput, Perak
places.note: Where three planters were killed on 16 June 1948.

places.name: Fraser's Hill
places.note: Where High Commissioner Henry Gurney was ambushed and killed on 6 October 1951.

places.name: Baling, Kedah
places.note: Where Tunku Abdul Rahman met Chin Peng in December 1955; the talks failed.

people.name: Chin Peng (Ong Boon Hua)
people.role: secretary-general of the Malayan Communist Party; had been awarded an OBE for wartime resistance against Japan, which was later revoked

people.name: Harold Briggs
people.role: Director of Operations whose 1950 plan moved half a million people into New Villages

people.name: Henry Gurney
people.role: High Commissioner, ambushed and killed on the road to Fraser's Hill in 1951

people.name: Gerald Templer
people.role: High Commissioner 1952-54; combined resettlement, food control, collective punishment and a promise of independence

people.name: Tunku Abdul Rahman
people.role: met Chin Peng at Baling in 1955, refused to legalise the party, and took the country to independence in 1957

toll.note: Malayan government figures: 6,710 insurgents, 1,346 Malayan police and soldiers, 519 Commonwealth troops and 2,478 civilians killed, with 810 civilians missing. Resettlement estimates range from about 400,000 to 573,000 people; deaths from disease and hunger inside the New Villages were never counted.

pedagogy.hook: It was called an Emergency, not a war, because insurance policies on rubber estates paid out for emergencies and not for wars.

misconception.belief: Britain left its colonies peacefully unless it was defeated.
misconception.correction: In Malaya Britain fought for twelve years, moved half a million people behind wire, deported 30,000 to China, used collective punishment and mandatory death sentences — and then handed the country over in 1957 to politicians it preferred, three years before the fighting stopped. Winning and leaving were the same policy.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Malaya is the case that breaks the simple story in both directions: the exit was negotiated and the war was real, and the two were parts of one strategy.

evidence.author: Karl Hack
evidence.work: The Malayan Emergency: Revolution and Counterinsurgency at the End of Empire
evidence.supports: The conduct of the campaign, the resettlement programme and the casualty figures.

evidence.author: Tim Harper
evidence.work: The End of Empire and the Making of Malaya
evidence.supports: The social and political context of the Emergency and its relation to independence.

contested.note: How much the New Villages were protection and how much punishment is argued about, as is whether British methods were genuinely less brutal than those used in Kenya. Karl Hack's work has revised earlier accounts that credited Templer's 'hearts and minds' with more than the record supports.

events.title: The Batang Kali killings
events.summary: A patrol of the 2nd Scots Guards surrounded a rubber estate settlement at Batang Kali in Selangor, separated the men from the women and children, and shot 24 unarmed villagers. The army said they were fleeing detainees; survivors and later witnesses said they were killed in groups.
events.significance: The most serious documented British killing of civilians in the Malayan Emergency. No one was prosecuted; a 1970 investigation was closed, and in 2012 and 2018 British courts accepted that the killings might have been unlawful while refusing to order a public inquiry.

places.name: Sungai Rimoh, Batang Kali
places.note: The rubber estate settlement where the killings took place.

people.name: Chong Koon Ying
people.role: survivor and campaigner who spent decades seeking an inquiry into the deaths of her family

people.name: Tham Yong
people.role: survivor whose testimony formed the basis of later legal claims

toll.note: Twenty-four unarmed villagers were shot. The number is not disputed; the circumstances are. The Scots Guards' account of prisoners escaping was contradicted by survivors and, in 1970, by several former guardsmen who spoke to the press.

pedagogy.hook: Twenty-four unarmed men were shot at Batang Kali in 1948. Seventy-five years later no British court has yet held an inquiry into how it happened.

misconception.belief: British counter-insurgency in Malaya was restrained, especially compared with what other powers did.
misconception.correction: British forces in Malaya used collective punishment, mass detention, deportation, mandatory death sentences and, at Batang Kali, killed 24 unarmed civilians in a single morning. The comparison with other empires is a separate question from the record itself.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the test case for how Britain deals with its own colonial record: investigations opened and closed in 1948, 1970 and 1993, court proceedings up to the Supreme Court in 2012 and the European Court of Human Rights in 2018, and still no inquiry.

evidence.author: Christopher Hale
evidence.work: Massacre in Malaya: Exposing Britain's My Lai
evidence.supports: The killings, the successive investigations and the legal campaign.

contested.note: The British government has never accepted that the killings were unlawful. Survivors, the 1970 guardsmen's testimony and subsequent scholarship hold that the men were killed deliberately; the official position remains that the deaths occurred while prisoners were escaping.

events.title: Merdeka: the independence of Malaya
events.summary: At midnight the Union flag came down in Kuala Lumpur and Tunku Abdul Rahman led the crowd in seven shouts of Merdeka. Eleven states became one independent country, with a rotating elected king, Islam as the religion of the federation and Malay as its national language.
events.significance: The first negotiated independence in British South-East Asia, achieved while an Emergency was still running, on a bargain between Malay, Chinese and Indian parties: citizenship for non-Malays in exchange for a special constitutional position for Malays.

places.name: Merdeka Stadium, Kuala Lumpur
places.note: Where independence was proclaimed on the morning of 31 August 1957.

places.name: Padang Bandar Hilir, Malacca
places.note: Where the Tunku announced in February 1956 that independence was coming.

people.name: Tunku Abdul Rahman
people.role: first Prime Minister; led the London talks of January-February 1956

people.name: Tan Cheng Lock
people.role: founder of the Malayan Chinese Association and architect of the inter-communal Alliance

people.name: V. T. Sambanthan
people.role: leader of the Malayan Indian Congress

people.name: Lord Reid
people.role: chaired the commission that drafted the independence constitution

people.name: Ahmad Boestamam
people.role: left-wing nationalist of the banned Malay Nationalist Party, detained for years and excluded from the settlement

pedagogy.hook: Independence was proclaimed while the war against the communists was still running, and would run for another three years.

misconception.belief: Independence movements were united fronts of a whole people against Britain.
misconception.correction: Malaya's independence was won by a coalition of three communal parties that Britain found acceptable, while the Malay left and the communists were banned, detained or in the jungle. Who inherits the state at independence is a separate question from who fought for it.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It fixed the terms of Malaysian politics for the next seventy years: a bargain in which citizenship was traded for constitutional privilege, written into Articles 152 and 153 and argued about ever since.

evidence.author: Tim Harper
evidence.work: The End of Empire and the Making of Malaya
evidence.supports: The negotiations, the constitutional settlement and who was excluded from it.

events.title: The Sarawak anti-cession movement
events.summary: When the last White Rajah sold Sarawak to Britain, the Council Negri approved it by 19 votes to 16 and 338 Malay civil servants resigned in protest. On 3 December 1949 a seventeen-year-old, Rosli Dhobi, stabbed the new Governor at Sibu; four young men were hanged in 1950.
events.significance: The only sustained popular resistance anywhere to a British territory being taken after the Second World War. It is also the reason arguments about Sarawak's constitutional status inside Malaysia still reach back to 1946.

places.name: Kuching
places.note: Where the Council Negri voted 19-16 for cession.

places.name: Sibu
places.note: Where Governor Duncan Stewart was stabbed on 3 December 1949.

people.name: Rosli Dhobi
people.role: seventeen-year-old member of Rukun 13 who stabbed Governor Stewart; hanged on 2 March 1950

people.name: Duncan Stewart
people.role: second British Governor of Sarawak; died of his wounds on 10 December 1949

people.name: Anthony Brooke
people.role: the Rajah's heir, who opposed the cession and was banned from Sarawak until 1963

people.name: Charles Vyner Brooke
people.role: third White Rajah, who ceded the country for an annual payment

toll.note: Governor Stewart and the four young men hanged for his killing: Rosli Dhobi, Morshidi Sidek, Bujang Suntong and Awang Rambli. Several hundred more were dismissed from government service or detained.

pedagogy.hook: In 1946 an English family sold a country. Three hundred and thirty-eight of its civil servants resigned, and three years later a schoolboy killed the governor who came to run it.

misconception.belief: After 1945 the British empire was only ever shrinking.
misconception.correction: Sarawak became a British colony on 1 July 1946, one year after the war and thirteen months before India became independent. It was Britain's newest colony, it was taken against the wishes of a large part of its population, and the men who resisted were hanged.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the sharpest counter-example to the idea of an orderly retreat from empire, and the origin of Sarawak's insistence that it entered Malaysia as a partner rather than a province.

evidence.author: Vernon L. Porritt
evidence.work: British Colonial Rule in Sarawak, 1946-1963
evidence.supports: The cession, the anti-cession movement and its suppression.

events.title: The Brunei revolt
events.summary: The Parti Rakyat Brunei, which had won every elected seat in the 1962 council election and had never been allowed to form a government, rose in revolt with an armed wing calling itself the North Kalimantan National Army. British and Gurkha troops flown from Singapore crushed it in about a week.
events.significance: It ended any prospect of Brunei joining Malaysia, entrenched the Sultan's personal rule under an emergency that has never been lifted, and gave Indonesia its opening for Confrontation against the new federation the following year.

places.name: Brunei Town (Bandar Seri Begawan)
places.note: Where the revolt began before dawn on 8 December 1962.

places.name: Seria
places.note: The oilfield the rebels seized, taking European hostages.

places.name: Limbang
places.note: Retaken by Royal Marines on 12 December after the rebels held hostages there.

people.name: A. M. Azahari
people.role: leader of the Parti Rakyat Brunei; was in Manila when the rising began and lived the rest of his life in exile in Indonesia

people.name: Yassin Affandi
people.role: military commander of the rising; captured in 1963 and held for many years

people.name: Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddien III
people.role: called in British troops, then ruled under emergency powers and kept Brunei out of Malaysia

toll.note: Dozens were killed among the rebels and the British-led troops in about a week of fighting, and several thousand people were detained; some leaders were held without trial into the 1970s. Published casualty figures differ and no agreed total exists.

pedagogy.hook: A party won every elected seat in Brunei's only election, was never allowed to govern, rose in revolt — and the emergency declared to crush it is still in force today.

misconception.belief: British intervention after 1945 was about stopping communism.
misconception.correction: The Parti Rakyat Brunei was a nationalist party that wanted a united independent North Kalimantan of Brunei, Sarawak and Sabah, and it had just won an election. Britain's troops restored a Sultan who then governed by decree. What was defended was a friendly ruler and an oilfield.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Brunei shows the last phase of British power in Asia doing what the first phase did: choosing which local ruler to back, and making his authority permanent.

evidence.author: Graham Saunders
evidence.work: A History of Brunei
evidence.supports: The 1962 election, the revolt and the emergency that followed.

contested.note: Casualty and detention figures for the revolt vary widely between British military accounts, Brunei government statements and later accounts by former Parti Rakyat members. No independent count was ever made.

events.title: The formation of Malaysia
events.summary: Malaya, Singapore, Sarawak and North Borneo joined to form Malaysia. Brunei stayed out. The date was postponed from 31 August so a United Nations mission could test Borneo opinion, after Indonesia and the Philippines objected that the people had not been asked.
events.significance: It ended British rule in Singapore and British Borneo in a single day, dissolving three colonies into a new federation rather than three new states — a solution Britain preferred because it kept the region defensible and out of Indonesian or communist hands.

places.name: Kuala Lumpur
places.note: Capital of the new federation.

places.name: Kuching
places.note: Where the Cobbold Commission took submissions in 1962.

places.name: Jesselton (Kota Kinabalu)
places.note: Capital of North Borneo, which entered with twenty conditions attached.

people.name: Tunku Abdul Rahman
people.role: proposed the federation in a speech in Singapore on 27 May 1961 and became its first Prime Minister

people.name: Lee Kuan Yew
people.role: Prime Minister of Singapore, for whom merger was the route out of colonial rule

people.name: Donald Stephens
people.role: led the North Borneo delegation and negotiated the twenty points

people.name: Temenggong Jugah anak Barieng
people.role: paramount Iban chief who signed for Sarawak

people.name: Sukarno
people.role: President of Indonesia, who called Malaysia a neo-colonial creation and launched Confrontation against it

pedagogy.hook: Malaysia Day was pushed back sixteen days so the United Nations could ask the people of Borneo whether they wanted to be in it.

misconception.belief: Decolonisation produced one new country per colony.
misconception.correction: Three British territories — Singapore, Sarawak and North Borneo — left the empire on the same day by joining an existing country. Two years later one of them was expelled and became a separate state after all. The map at the end of empire was made by negotiation, not by a rule.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Malaysia's formation is where students can see decolonisation being designed: Britain shaping a successor state it could live with, and the people of Borneo attaching twenty conditions in writing that are still litigated today.

evidence.author: Matthew Jones
evidence.work: Conflict and Confrontation in South East Asia, 1961-1965: Britain, the United States and the Creation of Malaysia
evidence.supports: The making of Malaysia, British and American motives and the international objections.

contested.note: Whether Sabah and Sarawak consented is still argued in Malaysian politics. There was no referendum: the Cobbold Commission of 1962 took submissions and the 1963 UN mission surveyed opinion. Supporters call this sufficient; critics call it a managed consultation.

events.title: Confrontation: Indonesia against Malaysia
events.summary: Indonesia opposed the formation of Malaysia as a British neo-colonial project and fought an undeclared war along the Borneo border, with raids into Sarawak and Sabah and landings in Johor and Singapore. British, Gurkha, Australian and New Zealand troops fought it to a standstill.
events.significance: Britain's last major military campaign east of Suez, fought to defend a country it had just created. It ended after Sukarno's fall, and the cost of keeping 60,000 troops in the region helped push London into announcing withdrawal from east of Suez in 1968.

places.name: Long Jawi, Sarawak
places.note: Site of an Indonesian raid on a border post in September 1963.

places.name: MacDonald House, Singapore
places.note: Bombed on 10 March 1965, killing three people.

people.name: Sukarno
people.role: President of Indonesia, who declared Confrontation and fell from power in 1965-66

people.name: Walter Walker
people.role: British Director of Operations in Borneo; ran the cross-border Claret operations that were kept secret for years

people.name: Tunku Abdul Rahman
people.role: Prime Minister of Malaysia throughout the conflict

toll.note: Usually given as about 590 Indonesian, 114 Commonwealth and 36 civilian deaths, with several hundred wounded. The figures come from Commonwealth records; Indonesian losses in the secret Claret cross-border operations are the least reliable part of them.

pedagogy.hook: British soldiers crossed secretly into Indonesian territory for three years in operations so classified that the men who died in them were reported as killed somewhere else.

misconception.belief: Britain's military role in Asia ended with the loss of India and Malaya.
misconception.correction: Britain kept about 60,000 service personnel in the region into the mid-1960s, fought Confrontation to defend Malaysia until 1966, and only announced withdrawal from east of Suez in 1968. Empire ended as a legal fact long before it ended as a military commitment.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows the last stage of the imperial retreat: Britain defending a state it had built, until the bill became impossible.

evidence.author: Matthew Jones
evidence.work: Conflict and Confrontation in South East Asia, 1961-1965: Britain, the United States and the Creation of Malaysia
evidence.supports: The origins, conduct and diplomacy of Confrontation.

events.title: Singapore's expulsion from Malaysia
events.summary: Malaysia's parliament voted 126 to nothing to remove Singapore from the federation after two years of quarrels over race, taxation and the People's Action Party's decision to contest peninsular elections. Lee Kuan Yew announced it on television in tears.
events.significance: The only case in modern history of a country becoming independent against its will. It also shows that the borders left by empire kept moving after the empire had gone: Britain had separated Singapore in 1946, joined it in 1963 and had no part in separating it again in 1965.

places.name: Singapore
places.note: Where Lee Kuan Yew announced the separation on 9 August 1965.

places.name: Kuala Lumpur
places.note: Where the federal parliament voted to expel Singapore.

people.name: Lee Kuan Yew
people.role: Prime Minister of Singapore, who had staked his career on merger and wept announcing its end

people.name: Tunku Abdul Rahman
people.role: Prime Minister of Malaysia, who decided expulsion was better than continued conflict

people.name: Goh Keng Swee
people.role: Singapore minister who negotiated the separation terms in secret

toll.note: The separation itself was bloodless. The communal riots in Singapore in July and September 1964 that preceded it killed 36 people and injured hundreds, on the police figures of the time.

pedagogy.hook: Singapore is the only country in modern history to become independent against its will — thrown out by a parliament that voted 126 to nothing.

misconception.belief: Singapore won independence from Britain in 1965.
misconception.correction: British rule ended on 16 September 1963, when Singapore joined Malaysia. The 1965 separation was a quarrel between Kuala Lumpur and Singapore in which Britain had no vote. Singapore's national day marks the second date, not the first.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows that the shape of post-colonial states was still being settled after the empire had gone, and by the people who lived there rather than by London.

evidence.author: C. M. Turnbull
evidence.work: A History of Modern Singapore, 1819-2005
evidence.supports: The merger, the quarrels of 1963-65 and the separation.

events.title: The Sino-British Joint Declaration
events.summary: Britain agreed to hand all of Hong Kong to China on 1 July 1997, including the parts ceded in perpetuity in 1842 and 1860. China undertook that Hong Kong's system, laws and freedoms would remain unchanged for fifty years under the formula 'one country, two systems'.
events.significance: The only time Britain negotiated the transfer of a major territory to another state rather than to its own people. Hong Kong's six million residents were not represented at the talks and were never given a vote on the outcome.

places.name: Great Hall of the People, Peking
places.note: Where the declaration was signed.

places.name: Hong Kong
places.note: The territory whose future was being settled.

people.name: Margaret Thatcher
people.role: Prime Minister; opened the talks in 1982 arguing the treaties were valid and conceded sovereignty by 1984

people.name: Deng Xiaoping
people.role: Chinese leader; told Thatcher China could take Hong Kong in an afternoon and offered fifty years of no change instead

people.name: Zhao Ziyang
people.role: Chinese premier who signed the declaration

people.name: Edward Youde
people.role: Governor of Hong Kong during the talks, who attended as a member of the British delegation and not as Hong Kong's representative

pedagogy.hook: Six million people had their nationality, government and future settled in a room they were not in, by two governments neither of which they had elected.

misconception.belief: Britain had no choice because the lease expired.
misconception.correction: The lease covered 92 per cent of the territory; the rest was Britain's under treaties China had never accepted. Britain gave up all of it because the ceded part could not function alone and because Deng made clear he would take the whole thing in 1997 regardless. The lease was the deadline, not the reason.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Joint Declaration is still a live treaty. Britain says China has breached it since 2020; China's foreign ministry said in 2017 that it is a historical document with no practical significance. Students can watch a colonial settlement being argued about in the present tense.

evidence.author: Steve Tsang
evidence.work: A Modern History of Hong Kong
evidence.supports: The negotiations of 1982-84 and the terms of the declaration.

events.title: The handover of Hong Kong
events.summary: At midnight on 30 June 1997 the British flag came down at the Convention Centre in Wan Chai, the last Governor sailed away on the royal yacht, and Hong Kong became a Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China.
events.significance: The end of the British empire in Asia, and the largest transfer of population from British rule to another state in the empire's history. It closed a colony founded in an opium war and handed it to the state whose predecessor had lost that war.

places.name: Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre, Wan Chai
places.note: Where the handover ceremony took place at midnight.

places.name: Government House, Hong Kong
places.note: Residence of 25 British governors from 1855 to 1997.

people.name: Chris Patten
people.role: the 28th and last Governor, who widened the franchise in 1995 and watched it dismantled at midnight

people.name: Jiang Zemin
people.role: President of China, who took possession at the ceremony

people.name: Tung Chee-hwa
people.role: first Chief Executive of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region

people.name: Martin Lee
people.role: democracy leader who spoke from the balcony of the Legislative Council building as the appointed provisional legislature took over

pedagogy.hook: At midnight the Legislative Council elected two years earlier was abolished and replaced by one appointed in Peking, and the last Governor sailed away on the royal yacht.

misconception.belief: Britain gave Hong Kong democracy and China took it away.
misconception.correction: Hong Kong had no elected legislature at all until 1985 and no directly elected seats until 1991, 150 years into British rule. The widened franchise came in 1994-95, in the last three years, after the handover date was already fixed. Both the lateness of the reform and its reversal in 1997 are part of the record.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: This is where the empire ends as a matter of dates: the last significant British territory in Asia, transferred not to its own people but to another state, in living memory.

evidence.author: John M. Carroll
evidence.work: A Concise History of Hong Kong
evidence.supports: The last decade of colonial rule, the handover and its immediate aftermath.
